Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 1–2:

(p-151)In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Tafsir (exegesis) of Surah al-Anbiya' (The Prophets)

This surah is Meccan by scholarly consensus (ijma'). 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud used to say: "Al-Kahf, Maryam, Ta-Ha and al-Anbiya' are among the first al-'Ataq (the earliest-acquired), and they are from my tilad (old, long-held possessions)," meaning: from the earliest of what I acquired and memorized of the Qur'an, like wealth that has been long held.

The Exalted and Majestic One said:

﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near for them, yet they are heedless, turning away.﴾ ﴿No new reminder comes to them from their Lord, but they listen to it while they are playing.﴾

It is narrated that a man among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was building a wall, when another man passed by him on the day this surah was revealed. The one who was building the wall said: "What has been revealed of the Qur'an today?" The other said to him: "Today there was revealed: ﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near for them, yet they are heedless, turning away.﴾" So he shook his hand free of the building and said: "By Allah, it will never be built, now that the reckoning has drawn near."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The reckoning of mankind has drawn near for them﴾ is general for all people, although the one referred to at that time was the disbelievers of Quraysh; what follows of the verses indicates this. His saying: ﴿yet they are heedless, turning away﴾ means the disbelievers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

What follows from this verse, regarding the disobedient among the believers, is their share of it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿No new reminder comes to them﴾ and what follows it is specific to the disbelievers. As for His saying: ﴿from their Lord﴾, one group said: the intended meaning is what is sent down of the Qur'an. His saying "new" (muhdath) means its coming down and its arrival to them (p-152), not that it is new in itself. Another group said: the intended meaning of "reminder" (dhikr) is the sayings of the Prophet ﷺ concerning the matters of the Sharia (divine law), and his admonition and reminding; it is thus "new" in the true sense, and his being described as "from their Lord" is because the Prophet ﷺ does not speak from desire, and says only what is from Allah. Yet another group said: "the reminder" (dhikr) is the Messenger himself, and they argued with His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿Allah has indeed sent down to you a reminder﴾ [al-Talaq: 10] ﴿a Messenger reciting to you the clear verses of Allah﴾ [al-Talaq: 11]. So it is "new" in the true sense, and the meaning of "they listen to it" (istama'uhu) is: they listen to him. His saying: ﴿while they are playing﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: their listening is in a state of play, so it is neither beneficial nor does it reach the soul.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 3–4:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿Their hearts are heedless. And they conceal their private counsel, those who did wrong: "Is this not but a human being like you? Will you then submit to magic while you see?"﴾ ﴿He said: "My Lord knows every word in the heaven and the earth, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."﴾

His words "heedless" (lāhiyah) are a circumstantial state (ḥāl) following another state (ḥāl). The grammarians differed over the parsing (i'rab) of His, glorified be He, words: ﴿wa-asarrū al-najwā alladhīna ẓalamū﴾. The position of Sibawayh is that the pronoun in His words "asarrū" is the subject (fā'il), and that "alladhīna" is an appositive (badal) of it, and that the dialect of "akalūnī al-barāghīthu" (the fleas ate me) is not in the Qur'an. Abu 'Ubayda and others said: the wāw and the alif are a sign that the subject is plural, like the tā' in your saying "qāmat Hind" (Hind stood up), and "alladhīna" is the subject of "asarrū." This is according to the dialect of those who say "akalūnī al-barāghīthu." A group said: the pronoun is the subject, and "alladhīna" is in the nominative by a verb whose implied form is: "asarrahā alladhīna" (those who concealed it), or "qālahā alladhīna" (those who said it).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Pausing on "al-najwā" in this reading and in the first reading is better, and it is not good in the second. A group said: "alladhīna" is in the nominative as the predicate (khabar) of an implied inceptive (mubtada'), its implied form being: "hum alladhīna ẓalamū" (they are those who did wrong), and pausing with this is good. A group said: "alladhīna" is in the accusative position by a verb whose implied form is: "a'nī alladhīna" (I mean those who). A group said: "alladhīna" is in the genitive position as an appositive (badal) of "al-nās" in His words: ﴿iqtaraba lil-nāsi ḥisābuhum﴾ [al-Anbiya: 1] (Their reckoning has drawn near for the people).

(p-153) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These are weak opinions.

The meaning of "asarrū al-najwā" is that they spoke among themselves in secret and private conversation, one to another. Abu 'Ubayda said: "asarrū" means "they showed," and it is among the words with contrary meanings (al-aḍdād). Then Allah, exalted is He, explained the matter about which they conferred, which is the saying of some of them to others: ﴿Is this not but a human being like you?﴾ Then some of them said to others, by way of rebuke for their ignorance: ﴿Will you then submit to magic?﴾, meaning: what he says; they likened it to magic. The meaning is: "Will you then follow magic?" ﴿while you see﴾, meaning: you perceive that it is magic and you know that, as if they were saying: "you go astray with clear proof and knowledge." Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to say to them and to all the people: ﴿My Lord knows the word in the heaven and the earth﴾, meaning: He knows these sayings of yours, and He is watchful over the recompense for them.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "Qul Rabbī" (Say: "My Lord"), while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "Qāla Rabbī" (He said: "My Lord"), in the sense of a report about His Prophet (ﷺ). The reading from 'Asim has been reported in differing ways. Al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: These are two widely transmitted readings in the recitation of the regional centres (al-amsār).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verse 5–8:

His, may He be exalted and majestic, saying:

﴿Nay, they say: "Confused dreams! Nay, he has invented it! Nay, he is a poet! Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier ones were sent."﴾ ﴿Not a single town that We destroyed before them believed. Will they then believe?﴾ ﴿We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the reminder (ahl al-dhikr), if you do not know.﴾ ﴿We did not make them bodies that do not eat food, nor were they immortal.﴾

When the verse before this one implied that they said, "What he has is sorcery," God, exalted is He, enumerated in this verse all that their groups had said. Each statement is introduced by a retraction (idrab) from the one preceding it, to show the confusion of their affair. It is thus a retraction from a previous denial, because the second statement is not真 in itself.

"Al-adghath" (confused dreams) means mixtures. The root of dghth (ḍigh th) is a handful of mixed grass and herbage, and the tangled features of a dream were likened to this, being that which cannot be interpreted and cannot be gathered into a coherent whole. Then he related the saying of those who said: "He is a fabricator who intends to lie." Then was related the saying of those who said: "He is a poet," which is the view of a common faction among them, because the noble ones of the Arabs did not fail to recognise at once that the structures of the Qur'an are not the structures of poetry. Then he related their proposal and their wish for a sign that would compel them and be in the utmost clarity, like the she-camel of Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) and others. His saying, ﴿as the earlier ones were sent﴾, indicates their knowledge that messengers came to the earlier nations.

As for His saying, ﴿Not a single town that We destroyed before them﴾, before it there is an implied statement that the meaning indicates. Its estimate: "The sign they asked for is Our custom: if a people disbelieve in it, We hasten their destruction. And no town from the towns in which this calamity descended believed; will these, then, believe?" His saying "We destroyed it" is a clause in the place of a description of "town." When a clause follows indefinite nouns, it is a description of them; when it follows definite nouns, it is a circumstantial state (hal) of them.

As for His saying, ﴿We did not send before you except men﴾, it is a reply to a group among them who considered it unlikely that God would send a messenger from among humans who would surpass his kind to this degree of excellence. So God, exalted is He, in His reply to them, cited the messengers from humans who preceded him. The majority read "yūḥā" (it is revealed) with the verb in the passive, while Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read "nūḥī" (We reveal) with the nūn. Then He referred them to asking the people of the reminder, since the Quraysh did not possess a Book nor any trace of knowledge.

People differed regarding the people of the reminder, who they are. It is related from ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām that he said: "I am among the people of the reminder." One group said: they are the rabbis of the People of the Book. It is related from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "I am among the people of the reminder," and one group said: they are the people of the Qur'an.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a matter that should be pondered. The dhikr is everything that comes as a reminder from God to His servants, so the people of the Qur'an are people of dhikr, and this is what ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, intended. But as for the one referred to asking them in this verse, it is not valid that they be the people of the Qur'an at that time, because they were their opponents. Rather, they were referred to ask the rabbis of the People of the Book, since they agreed with them in abandoning belief in Muḥammad (ﷺ). Thus their testimony, that messengers of old from among humans were not open to reproach, is binding upon the disbelievers of Quraysh.

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿We did not make them bodies﴾. It was said: "jasad" among things applies to what does not nourish itself, as in His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿a calf, a body﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 88]. So the meaning is: We did not make them bodies that do not nourish themselves. It was also said: "jasad" encompasses both what nourishes itself among bodies and what does not. The meaning then is: We did not make them bodies, and We made them, along with that, not eating food, like inanimate things or like angels. So ﴿We did not make them bodies﴾ is negated according to the first interpretation, and affirmed according to the second, with the negation falling on its attribute. His saying, ﴿they do not eat food﴾, is a metaphor for having a beginning (ḥadath). Then He negated immortality (khuld) for them, because it is an attribute of the Eternal, and everything created is not immortal in the abode of this world.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verse 5–8:

His, may He be exalted and majestic, saying:

﴿Nay, they say: "Confused dreams! Nay, he has invented it! Nay, he is a poet! Let him bring us a sign, as the earlier ones were sent."﴾ ﴿Not a single town that We destroyed before them believed. Will they then believe?﴾ ﴿We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the reminder (ahl al-dhikr), if you do not know.﴾ ﴿We did not make them bodies that do not eat food, nor were they immortal.﴾

When the verse before this one implied that they said, "What he has is sorcery," God, exalted is He, enumerated in this verse all that their groups had said. Each statement is introduced by a retraction (idrab) from the one preceding it, to show the confusion of their affair. It is thus a retraction from a previous denial, because the second statement is not真 in itself.

"Al-adghath" (confused dreams) means mixtures. The root of dghth (ḍigh th) is a handful of mixed grass and herbage, and the tangled features of a dream were likened to this, being that which cannot be interpreted and cannot be gathered into a coherent whole. Then he related the saying of those who said: "He is a fabricator who intends to lie." Then was related the saying of those who said: "He is a poet," which is the view of a common faction among them, because the noble ones of the Arabs did not fail to recognise at once that the structures of the Qur'an are not the structures of poetry. Then he related their proposal and their wish for a sign that would compel them and be in the utmost clarity, like the she-camel of Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) and others. His saying, ﴿as the earlier ones were sent﴾, indicates their knowledge that messengers came to the earlier nations.

As for His saying, ﴿Not a single town that We destroyed before them﴾, before it there is an implied statement that the meaning indicates. Its estimate: "The sign they asked for is Our custom: if a people disbelieve in it, We hasten their destruction. And no town from the towns in which this calamity descended believed; will these, then, believe?" His saying "We destroyed it" is a clause in the place of a description of "town." When a clause follows indefinite nouns, it is a description of them; when it follows definite nouns, it is a circumstantial state (hal) of them.

As for His saying, ﴿We did not send before you except men﴾, it is a reply to a group among them who considered it unlikely that God would send a messenger from among humans who would surpass his kind to this degree of excellence. So God, exalted is He, in His reply to them, cited the messengers from humans who preceded him. The majority read "yūḥā" (it is revealed) with the verb in the passive, while Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read "nūḥī" (We reveal) with the nūn. Then He referred them to asking the people of the reminder, since the Quraysh did not possess a Book nor any trace of knowledge.

People differed regarding the people of the reminder, who they are. It is related from ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām that he said: "I am among the people of the reminder." One group said: they are the rabbis of the People of the Book. It is related from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "I am among the people of the reminder," and one group said: they are the people of the Qur'an.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a matter that should be pondered. The dhikr is everything that comes as a reminder from God to His servants, so the people of the Qur'an are people of dhikr, and this is what ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, intended. But as for the one referred to asking them in this verse, it is not valid that they be the people of the Qur'an at that time, because they were their opponents. Rather, they were referred to ask the rabbis of the People of the Book, since they agreed with them in abandoning belief in Muḥammad (ﷺ). Thus their testimony, that messengers of old from among humans were not open to reproach, is binding upon the disbelievers of Quraysh.

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿We did not make them bodies﴾. It was said: "jasad" among things applies to what does not nourish itself, as in His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿a calf, a body﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 88]. So the meaning is: We did not make them bodies that do not nourish themselves. It was also said: "jasad" encompasses both what nourishes itself among bodies and what does not. The meaning then is: We did not make them bodies, and We made them, along with that, not eating food, like inanimate things or like angels. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 9–12:

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Then We fulfilled the promise to them, and We saved them and whom We willed, and We destroyed the transgressors.﴾ ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder. Will you not then reason?﴾ ﴿And how many a town did We shatter, which had been wrongdoing, and We brought into being after it another people.﴾ ﴿So when they perceived Our might, behold, they were fleeing from it.﴾

This is a warning, contained within His description of His way with the prophets, peace be upon them, that He fulfills their promises. Likewise, He will fulfill for Muhammad (ﷺ) and his Companions what He promised them of victory and the elevation of the Word. His saying, "and whom We willed" means: from among the believers. And "the transgressors" (al-musrifun) are the disbelievers who go to excess in their error and unbelief; and everyone who abandons faith is a transgressor.

Then He, blessed and exalted, rebuked them by His saying: ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder﴾. The Book is the Qur'an. His saying, ﴿in which is your reminder﴾ may mean: in it is the reminder that Allah sent down to you concerning your religion, your Hereafter, and your salvation from His punishment; so He attributed the reminder to them because it concerns their affairs. It may also mean: in it is your honour and your remembrance until the end of time, as great matters are remembered. In this there is encouragement. The encouragement is then emphasized by His saying: ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾, and this moved them to reflection.

Then He presented to them, by way of warning, the example of the nations of the past who were punished. "Kam" (how many) is for multiplicity, and it is in the accusative position governed by "qasamna" (We shattered). "Qasamna" means: We destroyed. The origin of qasm (shattering) is breaking physical bodies; when it is borrowed for a people, a town or the like, it signifies something resembling breaking, namely their destruction. He attributed these actions to the town, while meaning its people. This usage is common and widespread, and from it is: ﴿No town believed before them, [and yet] We destroyed them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 6]. His saying, ﴿and We brought into being after it﴾ means: We created and established another community other than the destroyed one.

(p-156) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when they perceived Our might﴾ is a description of a town from the towns mentioned in general terms at the beginning. It was said: it was in Yemen, called Hadura', to whose people Allah sent a messenger, and they killed him. So He sent against them Bukhtnasr (Nebuchadnezzar), king of the Children of Israel, and they defeated his army twice. In the third time he advanced against them himself, and when he defeated them and carried out slaughter among them, they fled running. It is also possible that the verse does not intend a specific town, but describes every town of the punished towns, and that the people of every town, when they perceived the punishment of whatever kind, began to flee. "Ahassu" (they perceived): they experienced it through the senses. "Al-rakd" (running): moving the foot in its well-known manner; and the fleeing or running one in general is a "rakid," whether it is an animal, or the earth, by way of likening it to an animal.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 13–16:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿Do not flee, and return to what you were made to enjoy in luxury, and to your dwellings, that you may be questioned.﴾ ﴿They said, "Woe to us! Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿And that continued to be their cry until We made them as cut stubble, extinguished.﴾ ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play.﴾

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Do not flee﴾ to the end of the verse may be from the words of the men of Bukhtnasr (Nebuchadnezzar), according to the narration mentioned earlier. The meaning on this view is that they deceived them and mocked them, saying to those fleeing from them: "Do not run away, and return to your places, that you may be asked for a truce or a poll-tax or some matter agreed upon." When they turned back, Bukhtnasr ordered that it be proclaimed among them: "O vengeance for the slain prophet!" And they were put to the sword, every last one of them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is related. It is also possible that ﴿Do not flee﴾ to the end of the verse is from the words of the angels of punishment, according to the other interpretation, that the verses describe the story of every town, and that He did not intend to specify Ḥaḍūrā or any other. The meaning on this view is that the people of these towns, through their delusion, saw themselves as held in a high position with Allah, and that if punishment or a command came to them, it would not descend upon them until they were disputed with or questioned about the reason for their denial of their prophet, whereupon they would argue with proofs that they supposed would benefit them. When the punishment descended, not in the manner they had hoped, and they fled running, the angels called out to them, mocking them: "Do not flee, and return to what you were made to enjoy, that you may be questioned, as you used to hope, through the folly of your opinion." Then His saying ﴿ḥaṣīdan﴾ means: by the punishment you run like cut stubble. ﴿Al-ītrāf﴾ means: luxury. ﴿Da'wāhum﴾ means: their supplication and their speech, i.e., they uttered nothing but lamentation. ﴿Al-ḥaṣīd﴾ is likened to the stubble of crops cut by the sickle, which destruction similarly cut down. ﴿Khāmidīn﴾ means: dead without spirits, likened to a fire when it is extinguished.

When the description of this state was complete, Allah the Exalted admonished the hearers with His saying: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play﴾, i.e., just as those who were struck by what befell them thought, and just as you disbelievers think now. So in the verse there is a warning in this respect, and the meaning is: We created all of this so that it may be taken as a lesson, reflected upon, and that one may believe in Allah in accordance with it.

Some people said: ﴿tus'alūn﴾ means: you will be made to understand and comprehended.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an interpretation the wording does not support. And a group said: ﴿tus'alūn﴾ means: something of your wealth and the goods of your worldly life, in mockery.

The meaning on this view is that they deceived them and mocked them, saying to those fleeing from them: "Do not run away, and return to your places, that you may be asked for a truce or a poll-tax or some matter agreed upon." When they turned back, Bukhtnasr ordered that it be proclaimed among them: "O vengeance for the slain prophet!" And they were put to the sword, every last one of them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is related. It is also possible that ﴿Do not flee﴾ to the end of the verse is from the words of the angels of punishment, according to the other interpretation, that the verses describe the story of every town, and that He did not intend to specify Ḥaḍūrā or any other. The meaning on this view is that the people of these towns, through their delusion, saw themselves as held in a high position with Allah, and that if punishment or a command came to them, it would not descend upon them until they were disputed with or questioned about the reason for their denial of their prophet, whereupon they would argue with proofs that they supposed would benefit them. When the punishment descended, not in the manner they had hoped, and they fled running, the angels called out to them, mocking them: "Do not flee, and return to what you were made to enjoy, that you may be questioned, as you used to hope, through the folly of your opinion." Then His saying ﴿ḥaṣīdan﴾ means: by the punishment you run like cut stubble. ﴿Al-ītrāf﴾ means: luxury. ﴿Da'wāhum﴾ means: their supplication and their speech, i.e., they uttered nothing but lamentation. ﴿Al-ḥaṣīd﴾ is likened to the stubble of crops cut by the sickle, which destruction similarly cut down. ﴿Khāmidīn﴾ means: dead without spirits, likened to a fire when it is extinguished.

When the description of this state was complete, Allah the Exalted admonished the hearers with His saying: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in play﴾, i.e., just as those who were struck by what befell them thought, and just as you disbelievers think now. So in the verse there is a warning in this respect, and the meaning is: We created all of this so that it may be taken as a lesson, reflected upon, and that one may believe in Allah in accordance with it.

Some people said: ﴿tus'alūn﴾ means: you will be made to understand and comprehended.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an interpretation the wording does not support. And a group said: ﴿tus'alūn﴾ means: something of your wealth and the goods of your worldly life, in mockery.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 17–18:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Had We wished to take a pastime, We would have taken it from Our own presence, if We were ever going to do [so].﴾ ﴿Nay, We hurl the truth against falsehood, and it crushes it, and behold, it vanishes. And woe to you for what you describe.﴾

The apparent meaning of this verse is a refutation of those among the disbelievers who said that the matter of Maryam and what resembles it is disbelief. Exalted is Allah above the saying of the falsifiers. The word "lahw" (pastime) in this verse means the woman, and it has been narrated that in some dialects of the Arabs it applies to a wife. The "in" in His saying ﴿if We were ever going to do [so]﴾ may be the conditional particle, meaning "if We were going to do [so]," and We are not so; and the theologians have here an objection and a resolution. It may also be a negative particle, meaning "má" (not), and all of this has been said.

The "truth" (al-haqq) is general, encompassing the Qur'an, the message, the Sharia, and everything that is true. Likewise "falsehood" (al-batil) is general in the same way. "Yadmaghuhu" (crushes it) means: it strikes its brain, and that is a fatal blow for a human being; so too the truth destroys falsehood. "Al-waylu" (woe) means disgrace and distress; it has also been said that it is the name of a valley in Hell, and this is what is meant in this verse. This is an address to the disbelievers who described Allah, blessed and exalted, with what is not permissible for Him and not befitting to Him. Exalted, blessed, sanctified and far removed is Allah above their saying. Rather, He is as He described Himself, and far above what His creation has described Him with; there is no lord other than Him.

(p-158) The word of the Exalted: ﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And those near Him do not disdain to worship Him, nor do they tire.﴾ ﴿They glorify Him night and day; they never slacken.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted, "*Wa lahu*" (And to Him belongs), may be a new sentence, or it may be set in opposition to His saying, "*Wa lakumu al-waylu*" (And woe to you). It is as if it were a division of the matter itself, meaning: for those who invent this claim there is woe, and to Him, exalted is He, belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth. The *lam* in "*lahu*" is the *lam* of ownership. "*Man fi al-samawati wa al-ard*" (whoever is in the heavens and the earth) includes the angels, the prophets, and others. Then He specified from this generality those among the angels whom He wished to honour, by His saying, "*Wa man 'indahu*" (and those near Him), because "*'inda*" (near) here does not refer to spatial distance but to a rank of honour. He, exalted is He, described them as not disdaining to worship God, nor growing weary of it, nor becoming exhausted in it.

"*Al-hasir*" (the exhausted) among camels is the one that has become tired, and from it comes the saying of the poet:

*Hunna al-wajā kam kunna 'awnan 'alā al-nawā*
*wa lā zāla minhā ḍāli'un wa ḥasīr*

(They are the hard-footed ones; how often they were a help against separation, and there remains of them one with a broken rib and one exhausted.)

"*Hasara*" (to tire) and "*istahsara*" (to become exhausted) have one meaning. This occurs in many verbs, even though the form *istaf'ala* (the tenth verbal form) is usually for seeking something.

His saying, may He be exalted, "*Lā yaftarūn*" (they never slacken). It has been narrated from Ka'b al-Aḥbār, may God have mercy on him, that he said: God made their glorification for them like breathing and the blink of an eye for human beings, occurring from them constantly without any weariness reaching them in it. Qatādah, may God have mercy on him, said: "It was mentioned to us that the Messenger of God (ﷺ), while he was sitting with his companions, said: 'Do you hear what I hear?' They said: 'We hear nothing of anything, O Messenger of God.' He said: 'Indeed I hear the creaking (*ating*) of the heaven, and it is right that it should creak. There is not a spot in it the size of a palm's breadth without an angel prostrating or standing upon it.'"

(p-159) His Exalted Majesty said:

﴿Or have they taken gods from the earth who can raise the dead?﴾ ﴿Had there been in them (the heavens and the earth) gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined. Glory be to Allah, Lord of the Throne, above what they describe.﴾ ﴿He cannot be questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.﴾ ﴿Or have they taken gods besides Him? Say: "Bring your proof. This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me." But most of them do not know the truth, so they turn away.﴾

This "am" (أم) is the one that is equivalent to the interrogative alif (ألف الاستفهام), and here it expresses affirmation and rebuke (تقرير وتوقيف). The view of Sibawayh (Sibawayh) is that it is equivalent to "bal" (بل) together with the interrogative alif, as if in the statement there is a turning away from the first matter, and Allah Most High confronts them with the words: "Have they taken gods who give life and create?" That is: your gods are not like this, so they are not gods, because it is among the attributes of a god to have power over giving life and causing death. A group read "yunshirūna" (يُنْشِرُونَ) with a damma on the yā', meaning: they give life to others. Another group read "yanshurūna" (يَنْشُرُونَ), meaning: they themselves come to life and their life endures. It is said: nashara al-mayyit and anshara-hu Allah (the dead man rose, and Allah raised him).

Then, blessed and exalted is He, explained the matter of mutual restraint (التمانع) by His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been ruined﴾. This is because some of them would have aggressed against others and gone off with what each had created. The concise statement on this is that if two gods were assumed, the disagreement between them over moving a body and making it still would separate them. It is impossible that both wills be fulfilled, and impossible that neither be fulfilled; and if one is fulfilled, the other's owner would be powerless, and this is not a god. The possibility of disagreement between them is equivalent to its actually occurring from them. There is another consideration: every part that comes out of non-existence into existence cannot be subject to two powers. If the power of one of them brings it into being, the other remains superfluous, with no meaning in relation to that part. The reasoning proceeds in this way, part by part. Then blessed and exalted is He declared Himself free of what the people of ignorance and disbelief describe.

Then He described Himself, exalted is He, as ﴿He cannot be questioned about what He does﴾. This description admits of two meanings: either (p-160) He means that by the right of His dominion and authority He cannot be opposed, and no one can question Him about anything He does, since He may do what He wills in His dominion; or He means that His actions are firm and that He places everything in its proper place, so there is no question or objection concerning His acts. These humans are questioned for these two reasons: because they do not possess dominion, and because there is much deficiency in their acts.

Then He, exalted is He, again confronted them about taking gods, and repeating this confrontation is an intensification of its denunciation and a demonstration of its corruption. In this confrontation there is an addition to the first, namely His saying: ﴿besides Him﴾. It is as if He confronted them here with the intent of disbelief in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and then called them to produce proof and evidence.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me﴾, it may mean by "this" all the revealed books, old and new; that is, there is no proof in them for taking gods besides Allah, rather they contain the opposite of that. It may also mean by His saying "this" the Qur'an, and the meaning is: in it is the mention of the earlier ones and the mention of the later ones. The mention of the later ones is by the call and the explanation of the Law for them and their guidance onto the path of salvation, and the mention of the earlier ones is by narrating their reports and mentioning the unseen matters concerning them. The meaning of the statement, according to this interpretation, is presenting the Qur'an as a demonstration of proof: that is, "Bring your proof; here is my proof, manifest in the mention of those with me and the mention of those before me." A group read "hādhā dhikru man wa dhikru man" with the genitive construction in both places; another group read "hādhā dhikru man maʿiya" with the genitive construction, and "wa dhikrun min qablī" with tanwīn on the second "dhikr" and kasra on the mīm of "min qablī"; Yahya ibn Sa'id and Ibn Musarrif read with tanwīn on "dhikr" in both places and kasra on the mīm of "min" in both places. Abu Hatim considered this reading weak, rejecting the kasra on the mīm in the first place, and saw no justification for it.

(p-161) Then He, Exalted is He, judged them that most of them do not know the truth, because of their turning away from it. There is another consideration: every part that comes out of non-existence into existence cannot be subject to two powers. If the power of one of them brings it into being, the other remains superfluous, with no meaning in relation to that part. The reasoning proceeds in this way, part by part. Then blessed and exalted is He declared Himself free of what the people of ignorance and disbelief describe.

Then He described Himself, exalted is He, as ﴿He cannot be questioned about what He does﴾. This description admits of two meanings: either (p-160) He means that by the right of His dominion and authority He cannot be opposed, and no one can question Him about anything He does, since He may do what He wills in His dominion; or He means that His actions are firm and that He places everything in its proper place, so there is no question or objection concerning His acts. These humans are questioned for these two reasons: because they do not possess dominion, and because there is much deficiency in their acts.

Then He, exalted is He, again confronted them about taking gods, and repeating this confrontation is an intensification of its denunciation and a demonstration of its corruption. In this confrontation there is an addition to the first, namely His saying: ﴿besides Him﴾. It is as if He confronted them here with the intent of disbelief in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and then called them to produce proof and evidence.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me﴾, it may mean by "this" all the revealed books, old and new; that is, there is no proof in them for taking gods besides Allah, rather they contain the opposite of that. It may also mean by His saying "this" the Qur'an, and the meaning is: in it is the mention of the earlier ones and the mention of the later ones. The mention of the later ones is by the call and the explanation of the Law for them and their guidance onto the path of salvation, and the mention of the earlier ones is by narrating their reports and mentioning the unseen matters concerning them. The meaning of the statement, according to this interpretation, is presenting the Qur'an as a demonstration of proof: that is, "Bring your proof; here is my proof, manifest in the mention of those with me and the mention of those before me." A group read "hādhā dhikru man wa dhikru man" with the genitive construction in both places; another group read "hādhā dhikru man maʿiya" with the genitive construction, and "wa dhikrun min qablī" with tanwīn on the second "dhikr" and kasra on the mīm of "min qablī"; Yahya ibn Sa'id and Ibn Musarrif read with tanwīn on "dhikr" in both places and kasra on the mīm of "min" in both places. Abu Hatim considered this reading weak, rejecting the kasra on the mīm in the first place, and saw no justification for it.

(p-161) Then He, Exalted is He, judged them that most of them do not know the truth, because of their turning away from it. The meaning is not "they turn away because they do not know," but rather: "they turn away, and for that reason they do not know the truth." Al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin read "al-ḥaqq" (الحق) with a ḍamma, meaning: this statement is the truth. Stopping on this reading is at "lā yaʿlamūn."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 25–28:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no god but I, so worship Me.﴾ ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honored servants.﴾ ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.﴾ ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not intercede except for one whom He approves, and they are, out of fear of Him, apprehensive.﴾

When He, blessed and exalted, informed them that they do not know the truth because of their turning away, He followed that with informing them that He never sent any messenger except that it was revealed to him that Allah, the Exalted, is One (fard), the Eternal Refuge (samad). This is a creed on which the prophets have never differed; they differed only regarding the legal rulings (al-ahkam).

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "nuhi" (نُوحِي) with a dammed nun, while the rest read "yuha" (يُوَحى) with a dammed ya', and there is a difference of reading transmitted from 'Asim.

Then Allah, the Exalted, after that enumerated another type of their disbelief. This is that, together with their taking of deities, they used to acknowledge that Allah, the Exalted, is the Creator and the Provider. However, some of them said, "He has taken the angels as daughters." The Christians said something similar concerning 'Isa son of Maryam, and the Jews concerning 'Uzayr. So this verse came refuting all of them and alerting to them. Then the Exalted declared Himself far removed from the statement of the disbelievers, turned away from their claim, and stated what the matter truly is in Himself with His saying: ﴿Rather, they are honored servants﴾. This expression includes the angels, 'Isa and 'Uzayr.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾, it is an expression of the excellence of their obedience, their worship, and their attentiveness to carrying out the command. As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾, meaning: what preceded of their deeds and actions and the events attributed to them, and what came later. Then He informed that they do not intercede except for one whom Allah approves to be interceded for. Some of the exegetes said: for the people of "There is no god but Allah." And "al-mushfiq" (الْمُشْفِقُ): one who is extreme in fear, burned by alarm over some matter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 29–30:

(p-162) The Exalted and Majestic One said:

﴿And whoever among them should say, "Indeed, I am a deity besides Him," We would recompense him with Hell. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿Have those who disbelieved not considered that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, and We separated them, and made from water every living thing? Then will they not believe?﴾

The meaning: "Whoever among them says such a thing," meaning, if he were to say it, for none of them actually said this. Some of the commentators said: what is intended by His words "And whoever says..." up to the end of the verse is Iblis.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, because it has never been reported that Iblis claimed lordship (rububiyyah).

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "najziihi" with an opening of the nun. 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid (Abu 'Abd al-Rahman) read "nujziihi" with a damma on the nun and on the ha'. Its basis is that the meaning is: We make it (Hell) suffice him, from your saying "ajza'ani al-shay'" (the thing sufficed me), then the hamza was softened to a ya'. His words "thus" mean: just as this speaker is recompensed, so is Our recompense for the wrongdoers.

Then He placed them before a lesson indicating the oneness of Allah, whose power is exalted. "Al-ratq" is that which is joined part to part, without cleft or opening, and from it comes "imra'ah ratqa'" (a woman without an opening, i.e. unable to conceive). The commentators differed over the meaning of His words, exalted is He, ﴿they were a joined mass, and We separated them﴾. One group said: the heaven was joined to the earth, and Allah parted them with air. Another group said: the heaven was joined part to part, and the earth likewise, and Allah parted them seven by seven.

(p-163) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On these two opinions, the "seeing" (ru'yah) that is referred to is the seeing of the heart.

Another group said: the heaven before rain is a ratq, and the earth before plants is a ratq, and Allah parted them by rain and plants, as the Blessed and Exalted One said: ﴿By the sky of the returning rain﴾ [al-Tariq: 11] ﴿and the earth of the splitting open﴾ [al-Tariq: 12]. This is a fine opinion, which gathers the lesson, the enumeration of blessing, and the proof by a perceptible, clear thing, and it fits His words, exalted is He, ﴿and made from water every living thing﴾, meaning: from the water that the splitting brought into being, so the meaning of the verse becomes clear and the reflection is directed. Another group said: the heaven and the earth were a ratq in darkness, and Allah parted them with light.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On these two opinions, the seeing is seeing with the eye, and "al-ard" here is a collective noun, so it is plural in meaning.

The majority read "ratqan" with a sukun on the ta'. "Al-ratq" is a verbal noun described by it, like "al-zawr" and "al-adl." Al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Abu Haywa read "kanata ratqan" with a fatha on the ta', meaning the thing that is joined (al-marthuq), like "al-naf" and "al-nafad," "al-khabt" and "al-khabat." He said "kanata" (they were, dual) in terms of their being two kinds. A similar usage is the verse of 'Amr ibn Shuyaym:

Did it not grieve you that the ropes of Qays and Taghlib have been severed, cut off from one another?

(p-164) His words "kanata" in the first two opinions are like your saying "Zayd was living" meaning: then he was not; and in the other two opinions they are like your saying "Zayd was knowledgeable," meaning: and he is so. Ibn Kathir alone read "a-lam yara" without the waw.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿and made from water every living thing﴾ make clear that it is not general in its universality, for the angels and the jinn are excluded from it. But the proper approach is to take it in the most general sense possible, so animals in their entirety, and plants, on the basis that life in them is metaphorical, are included in this. Another group said: what is intended by water is the seminal fluid (al-maniy) in all animals. Then He placed them before the abandonment of faith as a rebuke and reproof.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 31–33:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains lest it shake with them, and We made in it broad roads as paths, that they might be guided.﴾ ﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling, yet they turn away from its signs.﴾ ﴿And it is He who created the night and the day, the sun and the moon; each in an orbit they swim.﴾

"Ar-Rawasi" (the firm mountains) is the plural of rasiya, meaning steadfast, stable. It is said: rasa yarsu when it became firm and settled. It is used only of large bodies such as mountains, a ship, and the like. It is related that the earth used to tilt with its inhabitants until Allah, exalted is He, weighed it down with the mountains, and it settled. "Al-maid" means movement, "al-fijaj" are the wide roads among the mountains and elsewhere, and "subulan" is the plural of sabil. The pronoun in His saying, exalted is He, "fiha" (in it) may refer to the mountains (rawasi), and it may refer to the earth, and the latter is better. "Yahtadun" (they may be guided) means: in their paths and their dealings.

"As-saqf" is that which is high above. "Al-hifz" here is general, covering protection from the devils, from falling and collapse, and from other calamities.

"Ayatiha" (its signs) are its stars, its rains, the thunder, the lightning, the thunderbolts, and other things resembling these. A group recited "'an ayatiha" in the singular, which is intended as a collective noun.

"Al-falak" is the body that revolves in the rotation of the day and night; thus each of them is swimming and moving in it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Some of the exegetes have digressed into discussing what the falak is. Some said: it is like the iron of a millstone; some said: it is like a mill; and other such views that one should not presume to speak about. Nevertheless, we know that the falak is a rounded body. "Yasbahun" (they swim) means: they move about freely. A group said: the falak is a restrained wave, and they took His saying "yasbahun" to be from sibaha, which is swimming.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verse 34–35:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Had We not granted immortality to any human before you. So if you die, will they be immortal?﴾ ﴿Every soul shall taste death. And We test you with evil and good as a trial. And to Us you will be returned.﴾

It is said: the occasion of revelation of this verse was that some of the Muslims said: "Muhammad will never die; he is immortal." This reached the Prophet ﷺ, who denied it, and this verse was revealed. The meaning: We did not make anyone immortal, nor will We make you immortal. And no one should take vengeance upon you from the polytheists in this matter. Will they be immortal if you die, so that vengeance against you would be valid for them?

It is also said: the occasion of the verse was that the Meccan disbelievers criticised the Prophet ﷺ, saying that he was a human being, that he eats food and dies, so how could his being a messenger be valid? So the verse was revealed refuting them. The interrogative alif is placed within the meaning of the answer to the conditional, and it was placed at the beginning of the sentence because the interrogative has the front position in speech. The estimated sense is: "Are they the immortal ones if you die?" The fa' in His saying, Exalted is He, "afa-in" (أفإن), conjoins one sentence to another. A group read "mutta" (مُتَّ) with a damma on the mim, and a group read "mittta" (مِتَّ) with a kasra.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿every soul﴾ is a general term by which particularity is intended, and what is meant is every created soul. The word "dhawq" (الذَوْقُ, tasting) here is used metaphorically. "Nabluwkum" (نَبْلُوكُمْ) means: We test you. Evil is mentioned first because trial by it is more frequent, and because it is the custom of the Arabs to put the less and the worse first. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It leaves nothing small or great but that it has counted it﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾ [Fatir: 32], where He began the division of the nation of Muhammad ﷺ with wrongdoing. Al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that good and evil here are general, encompassing wealth and poverty, health and sickness, obedience and disobedience, guidance and misguidance.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of good and evil here is what can be a trial and a test: that is, the goodness and evil of wealth, the goodness and evil of the body, and the goodness and evil of worldly life. As for guidance and misguidance, they are not included in this, nor is obedience or disobedience; because the one who is guided, the very fact of his guidance is not a test, rather its goodness has been made clear. On this basis, there is in good and evil that which contains no test, just as there is also testing by commands and prohibitions, which is not included in this verse.

"Fitnah" (فِتْنَةً) means: examination and disclosure. Then He, Exalted and Majestic, informed of the return to Him and the rising from graves, and in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Us you will be returned﴾ there is a warning. A group read "turja'un" (تُرْجَعُونَ) with a damma on the ta', a group read "tarji'un" (تَرْجِعُونَ) with a fatha on it, and a group read "yurja'un" (يُرْجَعُونَ) with the ya' dammed, shifting from address to the third person.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 36–38:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿When those who disbelieve see you, they take you for nothing but a jest: "Is this the one who mentions your gods?" Yet they are disbelievers in the Remembrance of the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿Man was created of haste. I will show you My signs, so do not ask Me to hasten.﴾ ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾

It is narrated that Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and Abu Jahl ibn Hisham saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the mosque and mocked him, so the verse was revealed concerning them both. The apparent meaning of the verse is that the disbelievers of Quraysh and their leaders are all included in this sense: that they deny the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) taking up the matter of their gods and his mentioning their corruption. "In" here has the meaning of "ma" (not), and there is an ellipsis in the speech, its estimated form being: they say, "Is this the one who...?" His saying "yadhkuru" (mentions) is a word that covers both praise and blame, but the context of the speech always indicates the intended sense of the mention. The quotation of what He related from them is complete at His saying "your gods" (ālihatakum).

Then He refuted them by linking their denial of the mention of the idols with their disbelief in the mention of Allah, meaning: they are more deserving of blame, and they are the ones in error. His saying, "with the mention" (bi-dhikr), means: with that by which it must be mentioned, and "There is no god but Allah" (lā ilāha illā Allāh) is part of it. His glorified saying, "the mention of the Most Merciful" (dhikr al-Raḥmān): it is narrated that the verse was revealed when they denied this expression and said, "We do not know the Most Merciful except in Yamama." The apparent meaning of the speech is that "al-Raḥmān" was intended as a designation for Allah the Exalted, as if he had said, "and they are with the mention of Allah." This interpretation is more extreme in their misguidance and error.

His saying, the Exalted, "Man was created of haste" (khuliqa al-insānu min ʿajal), is a preparation for refuting them concerning their seeking of punishment with haste and their demand for a proposed sign, which is connected with a destroying punishment if they disbelieve after that. The Exalted described man, who is a generic noun, as being created of haste, and this is by way of hyperbole, as you say to an idle man: "You are of play and frivolity," and as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am not of Dadd, nor is Dadd of me." This is similar to the saying of the poet:

"And we, when we strike the ram a blow upon its head, the tongue falls onto the mouth."

As if they were people of striking the skulls and constant striking, so he said: they are of striking.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation completes the intended meaning of the verse, in that their haste is censured, and it is said to them as a threat: "The signs will come, so do not seek to hasten them." Some exegetes, regarding His saying, "Man was created of haste," said that it is in inverted form, as if He meant: haste was created from man, in the sense that it was made a nature among his natures and a part of his character.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation contains no hyperbole; it is merely a plain report. What led its proponents to it is their failure to see the aspect of figurative and metaphorical usage, so that the speech remains in its order. A parallel to this inversion which they said is the saying of the Arabs: "When Sirius rises, the sticks are level on the lizard," and as they said: "The she-camel was presented to the pond," and as the poet said:

"I withdrew my hand from the garment, taking it alone, dragged along the hands of those who ransomed."

(p-169) As for the meaning according to the one who saw the speech as inverted, it is like the meaning we have already presented. A group of exegetes said: His saying, "Man was created of haste," only intends that Adam, peace be upon him, was created by Allah the Exalted in the last hour of Friday, so haste came upon him before sunset. Some narrated that Adam, peace be upon him, said: "O Lord, complete my creation, for the sun is setting or has already set."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak opinion, and its meaning does not fit the meaning of the verse. Another group said: "al-ʿajal" means clay, and the meaning is: Adam was created from clay, and al-Naqqash recited:

"... and the palm grows between the water and the ʿajal."

This too is weak and differs from the meaning of the verse. Another group said: the meaning of "Man was created of haste" is, by His saying, "Be" (kun), so it is a state of haste.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This too is weak, for it specifies the son of Adam with something that every created thing shares with him. None of these statements has a meaning that is both sound and consistent with the verse except the first.

One group read "khuliqa al-insānu" with the verb in the passive form, and another group read "khalaqa al-insāna" with the meaning: Allah created man. The meaning of the verse as a whole, "Man was created of haste," is then in the sense of wonder at the haste of those addressed by this refutation. Then He threatened them with His saying: "I will show you My signs," meaning: what will displease you will come if you die upon your disbelief, intending the Day of Badr and other than it. Then (p-170) the Exalted explained their seeking of haste by their saying: "When is this promise?" Their question was by way of mockery and denial. And their saying, "if you are truthful," they meant Muhammad (ﷺ) and those who believed in him, because the believers were threatening them on the authority of the Shari'a. The position of "matā" (when) is in the nominative according to the Basrans, and some Kufans said its position is accusative as an adverb of time, with a suppressed verb whose estimate is: "it will be" or "it will come." The first is more correct.

The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 21, verses 39–41:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿If only those who disbelieved knew the time when they will not be able to ward off the Fire from their faces or from their backs, and they will not be helped.﴾ ﴿Rather, it will come upon them suddenly and confound them, and they will not be able to repel it, nor will they be given respite.﴾ ﴿And messengers before you were certainly mocked, but those who mocked them were encompassed by what they used to mock.﴾

The answer to "law" (لَوْ, "if only") has been omitted for brevity, since the context points to it. The extent of the punishment is left unspecified, because leaving it unstated is more eloquent and more awe-inspiring than stating it. Similar omission occurs in His saying: ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains were moved, or the earth was split, or the dead were made to speak...﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31]. The omitted answer in this verse may be estimated as: "when they hastened it," or something similar.

His saying ﴿when they will not be able to ward off the Fire from their faces﴾ (حِينَ لا يَكُفُّونَ عن وُجُوهِهِمُ النارَ) means the Day of Resurrection. He mentioned the faces specifically because of their nobility in the human being, and because they are the seat of the senses, and a person is most eager to defend them. Then He mentioned the backs (ظُهُور) to clarify that the Fire encompasses all their bodies.

His saying ﴿Rather, it will come upon them﴾ (بَلْ تَأْتِيهِمُ) is a corrective transition (istidrak, اسْتِدْراك), with an implied negation before it. Its sense is: "The signs do not come according to their demands; rather, it will come upon them suddenly." The pronoun refers to the Hour which will bring them to punishment, and it may also refer to the Fire. One group read "بَلْ يَأْتِيهِمْ" with the letter yā' (ي), so that the pronoun refers to the promise; and "فَيَبْهَتُهُمْ" with yā' as well, with the pronoun likewise referring to the promise. Al-baghta (البَغْتَةُ) means sudden surprise without any preceding warning. The word "yunzarūn" (يُنْظَرُونَ) means they will be delayed.

Then Allah the Exalted comforted Muhammad (ﷺ) with what happened to the other prophets: their peoples mocked them, and punishment descended upon the mockers. The word "ḥāqa" (حاقَ) means to descend and settle, and it is used for punishment and calamities. His saying "mā kānū" (ما كانُوا) contains an implied element, its sense being: "the recompense of what they used to do," or something similar. Along with this consolation given to Muhammad (ﷺ), it is also a warning to the disbelievers and an example set for him from the nations that passed before.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 42–44:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Say: "Who will protect you by night and by day from the Most Merciful?" Yet they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord.﴾ ﴿Or do they have gods that can defend them against Us? They are unable even to help themselves, nor can they be companioned from Us.﴾ ﴿Rather, We gave enjoyment to these people and their fathers until life lengthened for them. Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its extremities? Are they then the victors?﴾

The meaning: Say, O Muhammad, to these disbelievers who mock you and what you have brought, who deny the remembrance of the Most Merciful and are ignorant of Him: say to them, by way of rebuke and reproach, "Who will guard you?" The word "kala'a" (to guard, protect) means "hafiza" (to preserve), and from it comes the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: «Guard for us the dawn» (ikla' lana al-fajr). At the end of the statement there is an implied omission, as if He had said: "They have no preventer and no guardian." On this meaning the particle "bal" is used in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Rather, they are turning away from the remembrance of their Lord﴾. Then the questioning establishes against them that they have no preventer from Allah, by the disclosure of the matter of their gods. The meaning is: they assume that their gods, which possess this attribute, can protect them from Us; rather, none can protect them except Us. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿nor can they be companioned from Us﴾ may bear two interpretations: one of them: they will not be granted protection and will not be shielded; the other: nor will they be accompanied from Us with good or blessing, and the like. In the statement there is an implied omission, as if He had said: "There is none of all this; rather, these people have strayed because We gave them enjoyment and gave enjoyment to their fathers, so they forgot the punishment of Allah and assumed that their condition would never perish." The meaning of "life lengthened" is: life was prolonged in ease.

Then, exalted is He, He made them stand before the places of lessons among the nations and among mankind, according to the differences and the extremities. The "seeing" in His saying "Do they not see?" is seeing with the eye, followed by seeing with the heart. "We come" means: with power and might. "The land" is general in kind. His saying, glorified is He, "from its extremities" may either mean: what is ruined from the inhabited parts, and that is a part of the land; or it may mean the death of mankind, which is a diminishing of the generations, and in that case the intended meaning is the people of the earth. Some said: the diminishing from the extremities is the death of the scholars. Then He made them stand, by way of rebuke, before the question: "Are they the ones who overcome Him who overcame all the people of the earth and subdued all by His authority and majesty?" That is, such a thing is a manifest impossibility; rather, they are overcome and subdued.

His statement, may He be exalted:

﴿Say: "I only warn you by revelation, but the deaf do not hear the call when they are warned."﴾ ﴿And if a breath of your Lord's punishment touches them, they will surely say, "Woe to us! Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾

The meaning: Say, O you who make demands and overstep bounds: I only warn you by a revelation that Allah reveals to me, and by indications of the lessons that Allah has set up for you to contemplate, such as the diminishing of the land from its edges and other things. I was not sent with a constant sign, nor with what you demand. Then He said, "and the deaf do not hear," meaning: while you turn away from what I warn you of, so it is of no benefit to you. He likened their condition to the deaf.

Most of the qira'at (recited readings) have "وَلا يَسْمَعُ" with a ya' and the verb attributed to "الصُمُّ". Ibn 'Amir alone read "وَلا يُسْمِعُ" with a damma on the ya', a kasra on the mim, and "الصُمَّ" in the accusative. A group read "وَلا تُسْمَعُ" with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the mim, with the verb in the passive. Both of these readings put "الدُعاءَ" in the accusative. A group read "وَلا يَسْمَعُ الصُمُ الدُعاءِ" with "الصُمُ" annexed to "الدُعاءِ", and this is a weak reading, though it has a valid direction.

Then Allah, exalted, addressed Muhammad (ﷺ), threatening them with His saying: ﴿And if a breath of your Lord's punishment touches them.﴾ The nafha (breath, touch) is a passing stirring and a touch, as you say: nafaha bi-yadihi ("he swung his hand") when he moved it thus, striking in one direction. From it comes nafhat al-tib ("a whiff of fragrance"), as if it passes through the senses in fleeting moments. From it also comes nafaha lahu min 'atayahu ("he gave him a portion of his gifts") when he took a share of them for him. And from it comes nafaha al-faras bi-rijlihi ("the horse kicked with its leg") when it galloped.

The meaning: if a blow of punishment touches these disbelievers in their worldly life, they will surely regret and admit their wrongdoing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 47–50:

His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿And We shall set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything; and even if it is the weight of a mustard seed, We shall bring it. And We suffice as reckoners.﴾ ﴿And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion, and a light and a reminder for the God-fearing,﴾ ﴿those who fear their Lord in the unseen, and who are apprehensive of the Hour.﴾ ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down; will you then deny it?﴾

When He threatened them with a breath of the punishment of this world, He followed that with a threat concerning the setting up of the scales. He used the plural "scales" (al-mawazin), though it is one scale (mizan), because each person has a measure that is specific to him. He used the singular "justice" (al-qist), though it came in the plural form "scales," because "qist" is a verbal noun described by the word, as you say: "a people of justice (adl) and contentment (ridan)." A group read it as "al-qisṭ" with a ṣād. His saying, glorified is He, "for the Day of Resurrection," means: for the reckoning of the Day of Resurrection, or for the judgment of the Day of Resurrection, so it is by omitting a noun (taqdir hadhf mudaf).

The majority hold that the scale on the Day of Resurrection has a pillar and two pans, by which deeds are weighed, so that the perceptible and familiar thing among people is made clear to them. Lightness and heaviness are attached to bodies which Allah, exalted is He, will join to the deeds on the Day of Resurrection; these may be the pages of the deeds, or images that are created, or whatever Allah, blessed and exalted is He, wills.

Nafi' alone read "mithqalu" with a ḍamma, as a resumptive (mustaʾnafa) clause. The majority of people read "mithqala" with a fatḥa, meaning: even if the thing or the deed is of the weight (mithqal) of a mustard seed. The majority read "ataynā" meaning "we came (jiʾnā)." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and others read "ātaynā" meaning "and we brought (wa-ātaynā)" from al-muwātāh (agreement/complying). One cannot interpret "ātaynā" as "aʿṭaynā" (we gave), since it takes a prepositional particle (ḥarf jarr).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What weakens this reading is that changing a fatḥa-marked waw into a hamza is not well known; it is known only with a ḍamma or a kasra. In His saying, blessed and exalted is He, "and We suffice as reckoners," there is a threat. Then He, glorified is He, followed with the command concerning Moses, peace be upon him.

As for "al-Furqan," a group said it is the Torah, and it is "the light and the reminder." Ibn Kathir and Hamza read "ḍiʾāʾ" with two hamzas, one before the alif and one after it; the rest read "ḍiyāʾ" with a single hamza after the alif. Ibn 'Abbas read "al-Furqān ḍiyāʾun" without the waw; this is the reading of 'Ikrima and al-Ḍaḥḥak. This reading supports the view of those who say that all of it refers to the Torah. A group said that "al-Furqan" is what Allah granted him of victory, manifestation of proof, and other things by which He distinguished between his command and the command of Pharaoh, may Allah curse him; "al-Ḍiyāʾ" is the Torah, and "al-Dhikr" in the sense of reminding. His saying "bil-ghayb" (in the unseen) admits three interpretations: the first, that it means in their privacy and their solitude, and where no one observes them—this is the strongest of them; the second, that they fear Allah while His command is unseen from them, and they have only reasoned from indications, not from direct witnessing; the third, that they fear their Lord regarding what He has informed them of, of what is hidden from them, concerning the matters of their Hereafter and their worldly life. "Al-Ishfaq" is the most intense fear, and "al-Sa'a" is the Resurrection. His exalted saying "this" refers to the Qur'an, and "anzalnāhu" may mean "We established it," as you say: "the Devil sent down so-and-so in such-and-such a place" meaning he established him there; or the descent may be attributed to the angel. Then, blessed and exalted is He, placed them under questioning as affirmation and rebuke: is it right for them to deny its blessing, and what it contains of the call to Allah, exalted is He, and to righteous deeds?

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 51–58:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And We had already given Ibrahim his right guidance before, and We were knowing of him.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father and his people: "What are these images to which you are devoted?"﴾ ﴿They said: "We found our fathers worshipping them."﴾ ﴿He said: "You and your fathers have indeed been in manifest error."﴾ ﴿They said: "Have you brought us the truth, or are you among the jesters?"﴾ ﴿He said: "Rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them, and I am of those who bear witness to that.﴾ ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned away, retreating."﴾ ﴿So he reduced them to fragments, except a large one among them, so that they might turn back to it.﴾

"Rushd" (right guidance) is general: it includes his guidance to rejecting idols, and his guidance regarding the star, the sun and the moon, and other matters, including prophethood and what is below it. Some have said its meaning is: he was granted success in goodness while young. All of this is close in meaning. His saying, glorified is He, "min qabl" (before), means: before Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both. By this addition it is "before" in the same way as the relation of Nuh, peace be upon him, to him. His saying, exalted is He, "And We were knowing of him," is a praise of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, meaning that he deserves what he was qualified for. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]. The governing element of "idh" (when) is His saying "We gave" (ataynā). "Al-tamathil" (the images) means the idols, because they were in the form of a human being, made of wood. "Al-'ukuf" (devotion) means constant attachment to a thing. His saying "fatarahunna" (who originated them) is an expression about them as though they understand, and this is in terms of their being obeyed and submitted to; they have been described in several places with what is said of one who understands.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot﴾, to the end of the verse. It is narrated that a festival of theirs came, and a group of them resolved to have Ibrahim, peace be upon him, attend with them, hoping that he would find something of their affairs admirable. So he walked with them, but when they were on the road he resolved to stay behind from them. He sat down and said to them: "Indeed I am sick." So most of them passed by him. Then he said within himself in private: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols﴾, and a group of their weaker ones, who were walking at the back of the people, heard him. His saying "after you have turned away, retreating" means: to their festival. Then Ibrahim, peace be upon him, returned alone to the house of their idols, entered it, and with him was an axe. He found the idols standing, the largest of them at the front, then the one next to it, and then the one next to that. They had placed their food on that day before the idols, seeking blessing from them, so that they could return from that festival to eat it. Peace be upon him, he began to cut them with that axe and smash them, until he ruined all their shapes, except the large one, for he left it as it was and hung the axe in its hand and went out from it. "Judhadhan" means small pieces, and "al-jadh" means cutting. The majority read "judhadhan" with a dammah on the jim; al-Kisa'i alone read it with a kasrah; Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Nahik and Abu al-Sammak read it with a fathah. These are dialectal variants, and the meaning is one.

His, exalted is He, saying: "fa-ja'alahum" and similar wording is treating the idols with the status of one who understands, since they were worshipped and were placed in the position of one who understands. The pronoun in "ilayhi" (to it), the most apparent view regarding it, is that it refers to Ibrahim, peace be upon him; that is, he did all this intending that this might result in their returning to him and to his law. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to the broken large idol that was left, but the presence of the expression of hope in the statement weakens this.

**The Qur'anic text:** ﴿So they returned to themselves and said, "Indeed, you are the ones who wrong."﴾ ﴿Then they were overturned upon their heads: "You know well that these do not speak."﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you then worship, besides God, that which can neither benefit you at all nor harm you?"﴾ ﴿Uff to you and to what you worship besides God! Will you not then reason?﴾ ﴿They said, "Burn him and support your gods, if you are going to act."﴾ ﴿We said, "O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham."﴾ ﴿And they intended a scheme against him, but We made them the greatest losers.﴾

**The meaning:** What Abraham (peace be upon him) had said became clear to them, namely that the idols, which they had made fit for worship, should be asked and questioned. So they said, "Indeed, you are the wrongdoers" in having this man stand accused of this act, while you have with you those whom you could ask. Then they persisted in their misguidance, and by reflection and the immediate judgment of reason they saw that the idols do not speak. This led them, while they were speaking about him, to the point where the proof was established against them. His saying ﴿they were overturned upon their heads﴾ is a metaphor (isti'ara) for one who plunges into his error, as if he were turned upside down on his head, which is the most ugly posture for a human being. Likewise, this is their state in the worst condition of reasoning. So they said to Abraham (peace be upon him), when they were overturned in their bewilderment, ﴿You know well that these do not speak﴾, meaning: why then do you call to this? Abraham (peace be upon him) found at this statement a place for the proof, so he confronted them, rebuking them for worshipping images that benefit by their own essence neither nor harm. Then he belittled their status and disparaged them in his saying, "Uff to you."

[p. 179] Ibn Kathir read "Uffa lakum" with a fatha. Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read "Uffi lakum" with a kasra and without tanwin in both places. Nafi' and Hafs from 'Asim read "Uffin lakum" with a kasra and tanwin. "Uff" (أُفٍّ) is a word said in the presence of disgusting things, and so it is used metaphorically for disliked meanings, such as this one and others.

When Abraham (peace be upon him) overcame them through reasoning and proof, they lowered their heads, and pride took hold of them in sin, and they turned to the path of brute force and domination, and said, "Burn him." It is narrated that the one who uttered this statement was a man from the Kurds, from the nomads of Persia, that is, from its desert regions. God caused the earth to swallow him, and he remains sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿if you are going to act﴾ is an incitement (tahrid), as you would say, "Resolve upon such a thing, if you are resolved."

It is narrated that when their opinion united upon burning him, the king Nimrod imprisoned him and ordered that firewood be gathered. It was gathered over a period of months, for the sick would make a vow upon himself that if he recovered he would gather such and such a number of bundles, until there was collected from the firewood, both what people donated and what was brought to the king from the villages, something like a mountain of firewood. Then they set it alight. When they wanted to throw Abraham (peace be upon him) into it, they could not get close to it. Then Iblis came to them in the form of an old man and said to them, "I will make for you a device by which he may be thrown into the fire." So he taught them the craft of the catapult (manjanIq). Then Abraham (peace be upon him) was brought out, bound with ropes, placed in the pan of the catapult, and hurled, so that he fell into the fire. It had been said to the fire, ﴿be coolness and safety upon Abraham﴾, so only the rope that bound him was burned. It is narrated that Gabriel (peace be upon him) came to him while he was in the air and said to him, "Do you have any need?" It is related that he said, "As for you, no." It is also related that he said to him, "I am a friend (khalIl) of God, and I only ask my need from my Friend, not from His messenger." So God, exalted is He, said, "O Abraham, you have cut off the intermediary between Me and you, so I shall cut it off between Me and the fire. O fire, be coolness [p. 180] and safety." It is also narrated that when the fire was addressed, every fire on earth was extinguished. It is narrated that the crow used to carry firewood to the fire of Abraham (peace be upon him). It is narrated that the gecko (wazgha) used to blow upon it to kindle it, and likewise the mule. It is narrated that the 'adrafut (a kind of insect or lizard), the swallow, and the frog used to carry water to extinguish the fire. So God preserved this protection, and He let loose upon the others calamities and hands. Some scholars said, concerning what is narrated, that if God, exalted is He, had not said, "and safety," Abraham would have perished from the cold of the fire.

This is weak. The proper reading would have been that it be in the nominative case (marfu').
