He, Allah the Mighty and Majestic, said:

﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We had blessed for the worlds.﴾ ﴿And We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift, and We made each of them righteous.﴾ ﴿And We made them leaders guiding by Our command, and We revealed to them the doing of good deeds, the establishment of prayer, and the giving of zakat; and they were worshippers of Us.﴾

It is narrated that when Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was brought out of the fire, Nimrod had him brought before him and spoke with him. Then Allah sealed Nimrod's heart in disbelief, so he became obstinate. He said to Ibrahim, in the course of their exchange: "O Ibrahim, where are the armies of your Lord whom you claim?" He replied: "He will show you the action of the weakest of His armies." Allah the Exalted then sent upon Nimrod and his companions a cloud of gnats, which devoured them all, down to the last one, along with their animals, until the bones were seen gleaming white. One gnat entered the head of Nimrod, and so his head was struck with sticks and other things, and his torment by it continued for a long time until he died from it. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and his nephew Lot (peace be upon him) left that land as emigrants. That land was Kuthaa in Iraq. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was accompanied by his cousin and wife Sarah. On that journey he encountered the tyrant who intended to take her from him.

People differed concerning the land which was blessed, to which Allah delivered Ibrahim and Lot (peace be upon them both). One group said it is Makkah, and they cited the words of Allah the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds.﴾ [Al-Imran: 96]. The majority said it is the land of al-Sham (Greater Syria), which is the land Allah blessed. Regarding the religious aspect, it is blessed with prophethood and faith; regarding the worldly aspect, it is among the finest lands of Allah in soil, the sweetest in water, and the richest in fruit and bounty. It is the place known as the dwelling of Ibrahim and his descendants. It is also narrated that there is no sweet water on earth except that its source and its emergence are from beneath the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 74–77:**

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And Lot, We gave him judgment and knowledge, and We delivered him from the town that used to commit abominations. Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient.﴾ ﴿And We admitted him into Our mercy. Indeed, he was among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And Noah, when he called out before; so We responded to him and saved him and his family from the great distress.﴾ ﴿And We supported him against the people who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a people of evil, so We drowned them all.﴾

The estimate (al-taqdir): "And We gave Lot," so it is in the accusative by a concealed verb indicated by the apparent verb. "Al-hukm" is the decisive settlement of disputes between people. "Al-khaba'ith" (abominations) refers to men having intercourse with men and passing wind in their gatherings, besides their other disbelief. As for His saying about Noah, peace be upon him, "min qablu" (before), it is in relation to Abraham and Lot, peace be upon them both (p-183). "Al-karb al-'azim" (the great distress) is the drowning and the destruction that befell his people through his supplication against them, which was answered. His saying, glorified is He, "wa-nasarnahu" (and We supported him): since the greater part of his support was deliverance, and his people's defeat was not by his own hand but by a matter external to him, it was apt to say "nasarnahu min" (supported him against). The preposition "'ala" (against) is not used here as it is in the matter of Muhammad ﷺ with his people.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The mention of these prophets, peace be upon them, is a parable for the story of Muhammad ﷺ with his people, and the deliverance of the prophets and the destruction of those who denied them contains within it a warning to the disbelievers of Quraysh.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 78–79:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿And Dawud and Sulayman, when they judged concerning the tilth, when the sheep of the people strayed into it by night, and We were witnesses to their judgment. So We gave understanding of the matter to Sulayman, and to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge. And We subjected the mountains to glorify along with Dawud, and the birds too; and We were the doers.﴾

The meaning: "And mention Dawud and Sulayman." This is how a group of the exegetes have assessed it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It is possible in my view, and more strongly so, that the meaning is: "And We gave Dawud," coordinated with His saying "and Nuh" (21:76), and that is coordinated with His saying: ﴿And Lut, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 74]. The meaning according to this interpretation is coherent.

Sulayman was the son of Dawud, peace be upon them both, from the Children of Israel. He was a just king and a prophet who judged among the people. This incident occurred before him. His son at that time had grown up, and he used to sit at the door through which the litigants left, whereas they entered to Dawud, peace be upon him, through another door. A man who had a field of crops came to litigate before Dawud, peace be upon him. It was said that it was a vineyard.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The word "harth" (tilth) is used for both, but for crops it is further from metaphor. The sheep of another man entered his field and destroyed it. Dawud, peace be upon him, judged that the sheep should be handed over to the owner of the field. One group said: "On the condition that his vineyard remains in his hand." Another group said: "Rather, he handed the sheep over to the owner of the field and the field to the owner of the sheep."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

On the first view, it seems that he saw the sheep as equivalent to the produce that was destroyed. On the second view, he saw them as equivalent to the field and its produce.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

One should not suppose of Dawud, peace be upon him, anything except that his judgment was based on a well-directed reasoning. When the two litigants went out from Dawud, the owner of the sheep complained to Sulayman, peace be upon him. Sulayman came to Dawud and said: "O Prophet of Allah, you judged thus, but I have seen what is more gentle to all." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "That the owner of the sheep takes the field, tends it and repairs it until it returns to what it was; and the owner of the field takes the sheep during that period and benefits from their uses, such as milk, wool, offspring and other things. When the field is complete and returns to its state, each one returns the property of the other: the sheep return to their owner and the field to its owner." Dawud, peace be upon him, said: "You have been granted success, my son," and he judged between them accordingly.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

There is no doubt that Sulayman, peace be upon him, saw that what the owner of the sheep bears, through the loss of the benefits of his sheep during that period and the cost of repairing the field, equals what was spoiled in the field. His judgment excelled the judgment of his father in that it secured that the ownership of each of them remained over his property, and his soul would remain content with that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

One group held that this incident was not judged by ijtihad (independent reasoning), but that Dawud judged by revelation, and Sulayman judged by a revelation with which Allah abrogated (naskh, i.e., the cancelling of a previous ruling by a later one) the judgment of Dawud. Another group, among whom was Ibn Fawrak, took His saying, ﴿So We gave understanding of the matter to Sulayman﴾, to mean: "We granted Sulayman the decisive, abrogating judgment which Allah, blessed and exalted is He, willed to be established in the incident."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This group, in interpreting this expression, needs this strain, and the meaning remains unsettled for them.

Jumhur al-Umma (the majority of the community) said: Their judgment was by ijtihad. The scholars included this verse in their books on the question of the ijtihad of the two scholars. So it is appropriate to mention here a summary of the question of ijtihad. The people of the Sunnah differed concerning two scholars, or more, who issue rulings on the branches of the law (furu') and legal rulings on a question and then differ. One group said: "The truth in matters of the branches of the law lies on one side with Allah, the Exalted. He has established evidences for this and has urged the mujtahids (those who exercise ijtihad) to search for them and reflect on them. Whoever hits the sought-after determination in the question is correct absolutely, and he has two rewards: a reward for the ijtihad and a reward for the correctness. Whoever does not hit it is correct in his ijtihad but mistaken in not hitting the determination, so he has a reward and is not excused." This is what the Prophet ﷺ said: «When a scholar exercises ijtihad and errs, he has a reward». Likewise, it also falls under his, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying: «When a scholar exercises ijtihad and errs», where the scholar exercises ijtihad and contradicts a text that did not reach him, such as the saying of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab concerning marriage, that it is a contract, in the question of the tahlil (a marriage contracted to make a divorced husband lawful again) and the like. This combines his ﷺ saying «When a scholar exercises ijtihad and errs» with his saying: «Every mujtahid is correct», meaning: he missed the sought-after determination but was correct in his ijtihad. This group held that the mistaken scholar bears no sin for his error, though he is not excused.

Another group said: The truth lies on one side, but Allah, the Exalted, did not establish an evidence for it. Rather, He left the matter to the reasoning of the mujtahids. Whoever hits it, hits; and whoever misses it is excused and rewarded. We are not required to hit the determination; we are required only to exercise ijtihad.

The majority of the people of the Sunnah, which is what is preserved from Malik and his companions, said: The truth in matters of the branches of the law lies on both sides, every mujtahid is correct, and what is sought is only the best in opinion. Each mujtahid has been led by his reasoning to what is best in his view. The evidence for this view is that the Companions and those after them held differing opinions, and none of them saw that reliance should be placed on his own view over that of his opponent. Among this is Malik's, may Allah have mercy on him, rejection to al-Mansur Abu Ja'far of compelling the people to follow the Muwatta' (his book of hadith and law), concerning much of this meaning. When a scholar says about a matter, "It is lawful," that is the truth regarding that scholar, before Allah, the Exalted, and for everyone who takes his opinion. If another says, "It is unlawful," and all of that is by ijtihad, that is also the truth before Allah, the Exalted, regarding that scholar and for everyone who takes his opinion.

As for the one who holds that the truth lies on one side, he sees the case of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, as consistent with his view, and that Sulayman, peace be upon him, hit the sought-after determination, which is what he understood. And whoever holds that the truth lies on both sides sees that Sulayman, peace be upon him, understood the best and more preponderant judgment, not that the first was an error. On this basis they interpret the Prophet's saying ﷺ: «When a scholar exercises ijtihad and errs», meaning: he missed the better course.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Often the difference between the opinions on these questions is slight, but that slight superiority ennobles the opinion, and often the excellence between the two opinions becomes clear with minimal reflection. The questions of the branches differ from the questions of the fundamentals (usul) in this. The question of the two mujtahids in itself is a question of fundamentals. The difference between questions of the branches and questions of the fundamentals is that the discussion in questions of the fundamentals concerns the existence of a thing and how it is: as when we say, "Allah will be seen on the Day of Resurrection," and the Mu'tazila said, "He will not be seen"; and as when we say, "Allah is one," and the Christians said, "Three." Likewise: is there a sought-after determination in the questions? The discussion in questions of the branches concerns a thing whose existence is established, and how its ruling is, whether permitted or forbidden, and the like. The rulings lie outside its essence and existence, and are reached only through analogies and inferences. Questions of the branches are defined as whatever can be abrogated in part by another. Questions of the fundamentals are those in which, once one aspect is established, the other cannot validly arise as an abrogating one.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The question of ijtihad is long and branching, but this summary is suitable for the verse and calls for it, out of a desire for brevity.

Related to the verse is another section that must be mentioned: the return of a judge, after his judgment, from one ijtihad to another ijtihad that is more preponderant than the first. Dawud, peace be upon him, did this in this incident. The jurists of the Maliki school differed concerning a judge who rules on a case, then later sees that something other than what he ruled is more correct, and wants to annul the first and rule by the second. 'Abd al-Malik and Mutarrif, in the (book) al-Wadiha, said: "This is permitted to him as long as he is in his office. But if he is in another office, it is not permitted to him, and he is in the position of other judges." This is the apparent view of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, in the al-Mudawwana. Sahnun said concerning his return from an ijtihad in which he had an opinion to another that he saw as more correct: "It is not permitted to him." Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: "He begins the judgment anew with what is strongest in his view last." Sahnun said: "Unless he forgot the strongest view in his opinion, or was mistaken and ruled by another, in which case he may annul it." As for if he ruled by a judgment which was the strongest in his view at that time, then something else became apparent to him, he has no way to annul the first. [Sahnun said in the book of his son. Ashhab said in the book of Ibn al-Mawwaz: If his return to the more correct view concerns property, he may annul the first.] If it concerns divorce, marriage or manumission, he may not annul it.

The matter of the tilth was discussed earlier: one group narrated that it was a field of crops, and another group narrated that it was a vineyard.

"Al-Nafsh" is the straying of animals into crops or other things at night. "Al-Hamal" is their straying into them by day and night. Ibn Sida said: "Hamal" is not said of sheep; it is said of camels. And the judgment in Islam was established that the owners of livestock must compensate for what their animals destroy at night, because it is incumbent on their owners to keep them in check, and it is incumbent on the owners of crops and the like to guard them by day. This is the implication of the hadith concerning the she-camel of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, and it is the view of Malik and the majority of the community. In the book of Ibn Sahnun it appears that the hadith came concerning the towns of Medina, which are surrounded by walls, but as for the lands which are continuous fields without enclosure, and gardens likewise, the owners of the flocks must compensate for what they destroy by night or by day.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It seems that he went to the view that leaving animals unrestrained in such lands is a transgression, since they will inevitably cause damage. Abu Hanifa said regarding this: "There is no compensation," and he included it under the general meaning of the Prophet's ﷺ saying: «The wound caused by an animal is unpunishable (jubar)», and so he analogised all of its acts to its wounds.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge﴾. Some of them interpreted this to mean that Dawud, peace be upon him, did not err in this incident, but that in it he was given judgment and knowledge. Another group said: Rather, because he did not hit the sought-after determination in this incident, Allah, the Exalted, praised him by saying that he had judgment and knowledge to which he returned in cases other than this one.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And We were the doers﴾ is an emphasis on good and its confirmation. In the expression there is the meaning: "And that was in his favour and in the sight of one who deserves it from Us." It is as if He said: "And We were doers for the sake of answering that." And something was omitted for brevity, because the apparent wording indicates what was omitted from it. His saying "for their judgment" means Dawud, Sulayman and the two litigants, because the judgment is attributed to all of them, even if the aspects of the attribution differ. One group read: "for their judgment" in the dual form, meaning "for the judgment of the two of them".

People differed concerning His, the Exalted's, saying "yusabbihna" (they glorify). One group, which is the majority, held that it refers to his saying "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah). Another group, among whom was Mundhir ibn Sa'id, held that it means: they pray along with his prayer.

[Page 189]

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 78–79:

The words of the Exalted:

﴿And Dawud and Sulayman, when they judged concerning the tilth, when the sheep of the people strayed into it by night, and We were witnesses to their judgment. So We gave understanding of the matter to Sulayman, and to each of them We gave judgment and knowledge. And We subjected the mountains to glorify along with Dawud, and the birds too; and We were the doers.﴾

The meaning: "And mention Dawud and Sulayman." This is how a group of the exegetes have assessed it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It is possible in my view, and more strongly so, that the meaning is: "And We gave Dawud," coordinated with His saying "and Nuh" (21:76), and that is coordinated with His saying: ﴿And Lut, We gave him judgment and knowledge﴾ [Al-Anbiya: 74]. The meaning according to this interpretation is coherent.

Sulayman was the son of Dawud, peace be upon them both, from the Children of Israel. He was a just king and a prophet who judged among the people. This incident occurred before him. His son at that time had grown up, and he used to sit at the door through which the litigants left, whereas they entered to Dawud, peace be upon him, through another door. A man who had a field of crops came to litigate before Dawud, peace be upon him. It was said that it was a vineyard.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The word "harth" (tilth) is used for both, but for crops it is further from metaphor. The sheep of another man entered his field and destroyed it. Dawud, peace be upon him, judged that the sheep should be handed over to the owner of the field. One group said: "On the condition that his vineyard remains in his hand." Another group said: "Rather, he handed the sheep over to the owner of the field and the field to the owner of the sheep."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

On the first view, it seems that he saw the sheep as equivalent to the produce that was destroyed. On the second view, he saw them as equivalent to the field and its produce.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

One should not suppose of Dawud, peace be upon him, anything except that his judgment was based on a well-directed reasoning. When the two litigants went out from Dawud, the owner of the sheep complained to Sulayman, peace be upon him. Sulayman came to Dawud and said: "O Prophet of Allah, you judged thus, but I have seen what is more gentle to all." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "That the owner of the sheep takes the field, tends it and repairs it until it returns to what it was; and the owner of the field takes the sheep during that period and benefits from their uses, such as milk, wool, offspring and other things. When the field is complete and returns to its state, each one returns the property of the other: the sheep return to their owner and the field to its owner." Dawud, peace be upon him, said: "You have been granted success, my son," and he judged between them accordingly.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

There is no doubt that Sulayman, peace be upon him, saw that what the owner of the sheep bears, through the loss of the benefits of his sheep during that period and the cost of repairing the field, equals what was spoiled in the field. His judgment excelled the judgment of his father in that it secured that the ownership of each of them remained over his property, and his soul would remain content with that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

One group held that this incident was not judged by ijtihad (independent reasoning), but that Dawud judged by revelation, and Sulayman judged by a revelation with which Allah abrogated (naskh, i.e., the cancelling of a previous ruling by a later one) the judgment of Dawud. Another group, among whom was Ibn Fawrak, took His saying, ﴿So We gave understanding of the matter to Sulayman﴾, to mean: "We granted Sulayman the decisive, abrogating judgment which Allah, blessed and exalted is He, willed to be established in the incident."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This group, in interpreting this expression, needs this strain, and the meaning remains unsettled for them.

Jumhur al-Umma (the majority of the community) said: Their judgment was by ijtihad. The scholars included this verse in their books on the question of the ijtihad of the two scholars. So it is appropriate to mention here a summary of the question of ijtihad. The people of the Sunnah differed concerning two scholars, or more, who issue rulings on the branches of the law (furu') and legal rulings on a question and then differ. One group said: "The truth in matters of the branches of the law lies on one side with Allah, the Exalted. He has established evidences for this and has urged the mujtahids (those who exercise ijtihad) to search for them and reflect on them. Whoever hits the sought-after determination in the question is correct absolutely, and he has two rewards: a reward for the ijtihad and a reward for the correctness. Whoever does not hit it is correct in his ijtihad but mistaken in not hitting the determination, so he has a reward and is not excused." This is what the Prophet ﷺ said: «When a scholar exercises ijtihad and errs, he has a reward». Likewise, it also falls under his, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying: «When a scholar exercises ijtihad and errs», where the scholar exercises ijtihad and contradicts a text that did not reach him, such as the saying of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab concerning marriage, that it is a contract, in the question of the tahlil (a marriage contracted to make a divorced husband lawful again) and the like. This combines his ﷺ saying «When a scholar exercises ijtihad and errs» with his saying: «Every mujtahid is correct», meaning: he missed the sought-after determination but was correct in his ijtihad. This group held that the mistaken scholar bears no sin for his error, though he is not excused.

Another group said: The truth lies on one side, but Allah, the Exalted, did not establish an evidence for it. Rather, He left the matter to the reasoning of the mujtahids. Whoever hits it, hits; and whoever misses it is excused and rewarded. We are not required to hit the determination; we are required only to exercise ijtihad.

The majority of the people of the Sunnah, which is what is preserved from Malik and his companions, said: The truth in matters of the branches of the law lies on both sides, every mujtahid is correct, and what is sought is only the best in opinion. Each mujtahid has been led by his reasoning to what is best in his view. The evidence for this view is that the Companions and those after them held differing opinions, and none of them saw that reliance should be placed on his own view over that of his opponent. Among this is Malik's, may Allah have mercy on him, rejection to al-Mansur Abu Ja'far of compelling the people to follow the Muwatta' (his book of hadith and law), concerning much of this meaning. When a scholar says about a matter, "It is lawful," that is the truth regarding that scholar, before Allah, the Exalted, and for everyone who takes his opinion. If another says, "It is unlawful," and all of that is by ijtihad, that is also the truth before Allah, the Exalted, regarding that scholar and for everyone who takes his opinion.

As for the one who holds that the truth lies on one side, he sees the case of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both, as consistent with his view, and that Sulayman, peace be upon him, hit the sought-after determination, which is what he understood. And whoever holds that the truth lies on both sides sees that Sulayman, peace be upon him, understood the best and more preponderant judgment, not that the first was an error. On this basis they interpret the Prophet's saying ﷺ: «When a scholar exercises ijtihad and errs», meaning: he missed the better course.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Often the difference between the opinions on these questions is slight, but that slight superiority ennobles the opinion, and often the excellence between the two opinions becomes clear with minimal reflection. The questions of the branches differ from the questions of the fundamentals (usul) in this. The question of the two mujtahids in itself is a question of fundamentals. The difference between questions of the branches and questions of the fundamentals is that the discussion in questions of the fundamentals concerns the existence of a thing and how it is: as when we say, "Allah will be seen on the Day of Resurrection," and the Mu'tazila said, "He will not be seen"; and as when we say, "Allah is one," and the Christians said, "Three." Likewise: is there a sought-after determination in the questions? The discussion in questions of the branches concerns a thing whose existence is established, and how its ruling is, whether permitted or forbidden, and the like. The rulings lie outside its essence and existence, and are reached only through analogies and inferences. Questions of the branches are defined as whatever can be abrogated in part by another. Questions of the fundamentals are those in which, once one aspect is established, the other cannot validly arise as an abrogating one.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The question of ijtihad is long and branching, but this summary is suitable for the verse and calls for it, out of a desire for brevity.

Related to the verse is another section that must be mentioned: the return of a judge, after his judgment, from one ijtihad to another ijtihad that is more preponderant than the first. Dawud, peace be upon him, did this in this incident. The jurists of the Maliki school differed concerning a judge who rules on a case, then later sees that something other than what he ruled is more correct, and wants to annul the first and rule by the second. 'Abd al-Malik and Mutarrif, in the (book) al-Wadiha, said: "This is permitted to him as long as he is in his office. But if he is in another office, it is not permitted to him, and he is in the position of other judges." This is the apparent view of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, in the al-Mudawwana. Sahnun said concerning his return from an ijtihad in which he had an opinion to another that he saw as more correct: "It is not permitted to him." Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam said: "He begins the judgment anew with what is strongest in his view last." Sahnun said: "Unless he forgot the strongest view in his opinion, or was mistaken and ruled by another, in which case he may annul it." As for if he ruled by a judgment which was the strongest in his view at that time, then something else became apparent to him, he has no way to annul the first. [Sahnun said in the book of his son. Ashhab said in the book of Ibn al-Mawwaz: If his return to the more correct view concerns property, he may annul the first.] If it concerns divorce, marriage or manumission, he may not annul it.

The matter of the tilth was discussed earlier: one group narrated that it was a field of crops, and another group narrated that it was a vineyard.

"Al-Nafsh" is the straying of animals into crops or other things at night. "Al-Hamal" is their straying into them by day and night. Ibn Sida said: "Hamal" is not said of sheep; it is said of camels. And the judgment in Islam was established that the owners of livestock must compensate for what their animals destroy at night, because it is incumbent on their owners to keep them in check, and it is incumbent on the owners of crops and the like to guard them by day. This is the implication of the hadith concerning the she-camel of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, and it is the view of Malik and the majority of the community. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verse 80–81:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And We taught him the making of coats of mail for you, to protect you from your violence. Will you then be grateful?﴾ ﴿And to Solomon the wind, violently blowing, running by his command toward the land which We had blessed. And We are ever Knowing of all things.﴾

Allah, exalted is He, enumerated among the blessings upon mankind that He taught Dawud, peace be upon him, the craft of making armour, and softened for him the iron, so he would make it with the most perfect craftsmanship, so that it would serve as a protection from war and a means of deliverance from the enemy. And "labus" (lubus) in the language means weapons, and from it come the coat of mail, the sword, the spear and other things. From it is the saying of the poet:

"And with me is a lubus for the weak, as if it were a horn upon the forehead of one with sheep, startled."

He means the spear.

Nafi' and the majority read "liyuhsinakum" with the yaa, meaning: "that Dawud, peace be upon him, or the lubus, may protect you." Ibn 'Amir and Hafs from 'Asim read "lituhsinakum" with the taa, meaning: "that the craft or the coats of mail on which the lubus was placed may protect you." Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "linuhsinakum" with the nun, meaning the action is attributed back to Allah, exalted is He. It is narrated that people used to make the strong among them a garment of iron plates, and its weight would cut down most people. A group read "al-Rih" in the accusative, meaning: "And We subjected the wind." Another group read "al-Rihu" in the nominative, as a beginning (mubtada') whose predicate is the preposition-phrase before it. It is narrated that the violent wind would blow over the throne of Solomon, peace be upon him, on which was his carpet; and wood and planks were extended around the carpet until it formed a throne carrying all his army and provisions. The wind would lift it from the ground into the air, and then the gentle wind would take charge of it after that, carrying it to wherever Solomon, peace be upon him, intended.

As for His saying: ﴿to the land which We had blessed﴾, people differed concerning it. One group said: it is the land of al-Sham, which was his dwelling place and the seat of his kingdom. This verse specified his departure on his journeys to his land, because that implies his travel to the places to which he travelled. The "blessing" in the land of al-Sham is clear in its aspects. Some have said: the violent wind is with respect to the reception, according to the custom of humans and animals in hastening toward the homeland, and the gentle wind was at the start, wherever he aimed, that is, wherever he intended; because that is a time of deliberation, planning and change of opinion. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: in the verse there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and the sentence is complete at His saying "to the land," and His saying "which We had blessed" is an attribute of the wind.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that He means the land toward which Solomon, peace be upon him, travelled, whatever it was, because he did not travel to any land except that he reformed it, killed its disbelievers, established faith in it, and spread justice in it, and there is no greater blessing than this. So it is as if He said: "To whatever land We blessed, We sent Solomon to it."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 82–84:**

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿And among the devils were those who dived for him and performed other work besides that, and We were watchful over them.﴾ ﴿And Job, when he called to his Lord, "Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾ ﴿So We responded to him, removed the affliction that was upon him, and gave him his family and their like with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers.﴾

It is possible that His words "yaghuwwasuna lahu" (they dived for him) are in the accusative position, meaning "and We subjected to him some of the devils." It is also possible that they are in the nominative position, as the subject of a new sentence. This fits the two recitations (qira'at) mentioned earlier in His words "wa-li-Sulayman al-rih" (and to Solomon the wind), which are read in the accusative and in the nominative. His words "yaghuwwasuna" (they dive) are plural in accordance with the meaning of "min" (some of), not its wording. "Al-ghawš" (diving) means entering into water and earth. "Al-'aml dūna dhalika" (work besides that) refers to building and other crafts, service and the like. As for His words "wa-kunna lahum hafizin" (and We were watchful over them), it has been said that the meaning is: protecting them from corrupting what they had made, for they had an eagerness to do so, were it not that God the Exalted prevented them from it. It has also been said that the meaning is: "watching over them" and "present with them," that is, none of them deviates from Our knowledge and Our subjugation.

As for His words, "wa-Ayyub" (and Job), the best reading of it is the accusative, by a hidden verb whose estimated form is: "and remember Job." The narratives about Job, peace be upon him, are lengthy and vary among the exegetes. The summary of this is that it has been related that Job, peace be upon him, was a prophet sent to a people. He had abundant wealth in camels, cattle and sheep, and he was the lord of al-Buthaniyya in the land of al-Sham (Syria). He remained in that state for a period. Then, when God, blessed and exalted, wished to test him and try him, He permitted Iblis (Satan) to corrupt his property. So Iblis sought help from his offspring, and they burned all his property and blessings completely. Whenever he was informed of any of that, he praised God the Exalted and said: "It is a loan which its owner has taken back, and the one who bestowed it." When Iblis saw that, he came and reported his failure regarding him. So God permitted him to destroy his sons and relatives, and he did all of that completely. Job, peace be upon him, persisted in thanking Him. Iblis then informed Him of his failure, so God the Exalted permitted him to afflict his body, and He restrained his tongue, eyes and heart from him. Iblis came while he was prostrating and blew a blast into his nose, and his body was burned by it. God made it a festering sore (akla) in his body. When it grew severe and began to rot, people expelled him from among them and placed him on a refuse heap (subata). No one remained with him except his wife. It is said that she was the daughter of Joseph the Righteous, and it is said that her name was Rahma. It is said about Job that he was from the Children of Israel, and it is said that he was from the Romans, from the offspring of Esau. His wife would strive on his behalf, come to him, feed him and attend to him. He remained in this affliction for a long period, said to be thirty years, said to be eighteen years, said to be twelve years, said to be nine years, and said to be three. In all of that he was patient and grateful, until there came to him, as has been related, three men from among those who had believed in him. They reproached him with harsh words, blamed him, and rebuked him, saying: "Your Lord has done this to you only because of the corruption of your inner self regarding you." Job replied to them at the end of their statement with words implying that he was humbled and could not establish a proof or clarify an injustice. So God the Exalted addressed him, rebuking him for this statement and making clear that no one has any argument against God, and that He is not questioned about what He does. Then He, glorified and exalted, informed him that He had permitted the improvement of his condition and had returned His favour to him. At that point Job, peace be upon him, supplicated, and his supplication was answered.

It is also related that Job, peace be upon him, remained patient and did not supplicate for the removal of what afflicted him. It has been related that worms would fall from him, and he would return them with his hand, until some people who had been hostile to him passed by and gloated over him. He was pained by that and supplicated then, and his supplication was answered. His wife had been absent from him on some of her affairs. God caused a spring to gush forth for him and commanded him to drink from it, so his inner body was healed. He was commanded to bathe, so his outer body was healed, and he was restored to his best condition. The finest garments were brought to him, and a swarm of golden locusts fell upon him, and he began to gather them into his garment. God the Exalted called out to him: "O Job, did I not make you independent of this?" He said: "Yes, my Lord, but there is no independence for me from Your blessing." While he was in that state, his wife came and did not see him on the refuse heap. She became distraught and thought that he had been taken away from her, and she began to wander about in bewilderment. He said to her: "What is your matter, woman?" She was awed by his fine appearance, so she said: "I have lost a sick man who was with me in this place, and the landmarks of the place have changed." During the conversation she looked at him closely and saw Job, and she said to him: "Are you Job?" He said: "Yes," and he embraced her and wept. It is related that he did not part from her until God showed him all his property present before him.

People differed about his family and children whom God had given him. It has been said: all of that was in this world, so God returned to him his sight and his children in their very persons, and He made their like a multiplied number for him in the Hereafter. It has also been said: rather, he was given all of that in this world, both family and property.

As for His words, "wa-dhikra li-l-'abidin" (and a reminder for the worshippers), that is: a remembrance and an admonition. None worships God except a believer. The reminder lies only in his trial, and the mercy lies in the removal of that. As for His words, "annī massanī al-durr" (that adversity has touched me), its estimated form is: "bi-anni massanī" (that adversity has touched me), so the preposition was deleted and "anni" remained in the accusative position. It has been related that the cause of Job's trial, peace be upon him, was that he entered with a people before a tyrannical king. The people spoke harshly to him, while Job spoke to him gently out of fear for his property. So God punished him for that. It has been related that he was asked: "Why do you not supplicate for well-being?" He would say: "Indeed, I am ashamed before God to ask Him to remove His punishment until there passes over me in it what has passed of ease." Affliction befell him, as has been related, when he was eighty years old.

This fits the two recitations (qira'at) mentioned earlier in His words "wa-li-Sulayman al-rih" (and to Solomon the wind), which are read in the accusative and in the nominative. His words "yaghuwwasuna" (they dive) are plural in accordance with the meaning of "min" (some of), not its wording. "Al-ghawš" (diving) means entering into water and earth. "Al-'aml dūna dhalika" (work besides that) refers to building and other crafts, service and the like. As for His words "wa-kunna lahum hafizin" (and We were watchful over them), it has been said that the meaning is: protecting them from corrupting what they had made, for they had an eagerness to do so, were it not that God the Exalted prevented them from it. It has also been said that the meaning is: "watching over them" and "present with them," that is, none of them deviates from Our knowledge and Our subjugation.

As for His words, "wa-Ayyub" (and Job), the best reading of it is the accusative, by a hidden verb whose estimated form is: "and remember Job." The narratives about Job, peace be upon him, are lengthy and vary among the exegetes. The summary of this is that it has been related that Job, peace be upon him, was a prophet sent to a people. He had abundant wealth in camels, cattle and sheep, and he was the lord of al-Buthaniyya in the land of al-Sham (Syria). He remained in that state for a period. Then, when God, blessed and exalted, wished to test him and try him, He permitted Iblis (Satan) to corrupt his property. So Iblis sought help from his offspring, and they burned all his property and blessings completely. Whenever he was informed of any of that, he praised God the Exalted and said: "It is a loan which its owner has taken back, and the one who bestowed it." When Iblis saw that, he came and reported his failure regarding him. So God permitted him to destroy his sons and relatives, and he did all of that completely. Job, peace be upon him, persisted in thanking Him. Iblis then informed Him of his failure, so God the Exalted permitted him to afflict his body, and He restrained his tongue, eyes and heart from him. Iblis came while he was prostrating and blew a blast into his nose, and his body was burned by it. God made it a festering sore (akla) in his body. When it grew severe and began to rot, people expelled him from among them and placed him on a refuse heap (subata). No one remained with him except his wife. It is said that she was the daughter of Joseph the Righteous, and it is said that her name was Rahma. It is said about Job that he was from the Children of Israel, and it is said that he was from the Romans, from the offspring of Esau. His wife would strive on his behalf, come to him, feed him and attend to him. He remained in this affliction for a long period, said to be thirty years, said to be eighteen years, said to be twelve years, said to be nine years, and said to be three. In all of that he was patient and grateful, until there came to him, as has been related, three men from among those who had believed in him. They reproached him with harsh words, blamed him, and rebuked him, saying: "Your Lord has done this to you only because of the corruption of your inner self regarding you." Job replied to them at the end of their statement with words implying that he was humbled and could not establish a proof or clarify an injustice. So God the Exalted addressed him, rebuking him for this statement and making clear that no one has any argument against God, and that He is not questioned about what He does. Then He, glorified and exalted, informed him that He had permitted the improvement of his condition and had returned His favour to him. At that point Job, peace be upon him, supplicated, and his supplication was answered.

It is also related that Job, peace be upon him, remained patient and did not supplicate for the removal of what afflicted him. It has been related that worms would fall from him, and he would return them with his hand, until some people who had been hostile to him passed by and gloated over him. He was pained by that and supplicated then, and his supplication was answered. His wife had been absent from him on some of her affairs. God caused a spring to gush forth for him and commanded him to drink from it, so his inner body was healed. He was commanded to bathe, so his outer body was healed, and he was restored to his best condition. The finest garments were brought to him, and a swarm of golden locusts fell upon him, and he began to gather them into his garment. God the Exalted called out to him: "O Job, did I not make you independent of this?" He said: "Yes, my Lord, but there is no independence for me from Your blessing." While he was in that state, his wife came and did not see him on the refuse heap. She became distraught and thought that he had been taken away from her, and she began to wander about in bewilderment. He said to her: "What is your matter, woman?" She was awed by his fine appearance, so she said: "I have lost a sick man who was with me in this place, and the landmarks of the place have changed." During the conversation she looked at him closely and saw Job, and she said to him: "Are you Job?" He said: "Yes," and he embraced her and wept. It is related that he did not part from her until God showed him all his property present before him.

People differed about his family and children whom God had given him. It has been said: all of that was in this world, so God returned to him his sight and his children in their very persons, and He made their like a multiplied number for him in the Hereafter. It has also been said: rather, he was given all of that in this world, both family and property.

As for His words, "wa-dhikra li-l-'abidin" (and a reminder for the worshippers), that is: a remembrance and an admonition. None worships God except a believer. The reminder lies only in his trial, and the mercy lies in the removal of that. As for His words, "annī massanī al-durr" (that adversity has touched me), its estimated form is: "bi-anni massanī" (that adversity has touched me), so the preposition was deleted and "anni" remained in the accusative position. It has been related that the cause of Job's trial, peace be upon him, was that he entered with a people before a tyrannical king. The people spoke harshly to him, while Job spoke to him gently out of fear for his property. So God punished him for that. It has been related that he was asked: "Why do you not supplicate for well-being?" He would say: "Indeed, I am ashamed before God to ask Him to remove His punishment until there passes over me in it what has passed of ease." Affliction befell him, as has been related, when he was eighty years old.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 85–86:

The Most High said:

﴿And Isma'il and Idris and Dhul-Kifl; each of them was among the patient.﴾ ﴿And We admitted them into Our mercy; indeed they were among the righteous.﴾

The meaning: Mention Isma'il, who is Isma'il ibn Ibrahim al-Khalil (the Friend), peace be upon them both, and he is the father of the Arabs who are known today according to some of them. Idris is Khanukh (Enoch), and he was the first prophet whom Allah sent from among the children of Adam. It is reported that he was a tailor who would glorify Allah (tasbih) when inserting the needle and praise Him (hamd) when withdrawing it. Dhul-Kifl was a prophet. It is reported that he was sent to one man only. It was also said: he was not a prophet (p-193) but he was a righteous servant. It is reported that Ilyasa' (Elisha) gathered the Children of Israel and said: "Who will undertake for me the fasting of the day, the standing in prayer at night, and not becoming angry, and I will entrust to him the judging of the servants after me?" A young man stood up and said: "I undertake that for you." He returned to him three times on this matter, and each time he said: "I undertake that for you." So he appointed him. When Ilyasa' died, he took up the affair. Iblis came to anger him, and he (Dhul-Kifl) used not to sleep except during the midday rest (al-qa'ilah, the midday siesta). So Iblis would come to him at the time of the midday rest for several days, wake him, complain of an injustice done to him, and intend to constrict his chest. But his chest was not constricted, and he went with him to render justice to him himself. When Iblis saw that, he despaired of him and departed, and Allah sufficed him against his evil. He was named "Dhul-Kifl" because he undertook a matter and fulfilled it. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 87–88:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿And Dhu'l-Nun, when he went off in anger, thinking that We would not decree (any hardship) for him. Then he called out in the darkness: "There is no god but You; glory be to You. Indeed I have been among the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿So We answered him and delivered him from the distress. And thus do We deliver the believers.﴾

The implied meaning: "Remember Dhu'l-Nun." Al-Nun is the fish (al-hut), and his companion is Yunus ibn Matta, peace be upon him. He is ascribed to the fish that swallowed him, in the state that will be mentioned in its proper place as the context requires. He was the prophet of the people of Nineveh (Ninawa). This is the one concerning whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says, 'I am better than Yunus ibn Matta,' has lied." In another hadith: "It is not fitting for anyone to say, 'I am better than Yunus ibn Matta.'" This hadith, and his saying: "Do not prefer me over Musa," lead one to suppose that they contradict his peace and blessings be upon him, when he said on the pulpit: "I am the master of the descendants of Adam, and I say this without boasting."

The resolution of this is in two ways. The first, which is mentioned by people, is that his saying "I am the master of the descendants of Adam" came later in time, and that this is a station which Allah the Exalted informed him of, which he had not known at the time of those earlier statements. The second way, which in my view is more fitting with the state of the Prophet (ﷺ), is that he was only forbidden from preferring between two named individuals, and he adopted the course of humility, while he remained the master of the descendants of Adam. Rather, he forbade that he be preferred over Musa, out of concern that the Jews would become angry because of it and their aversion to faith would increase. The occasion of the hadith indicates this: a Jew said, "No, by Him who preferred Musa over all the worlds," and a man of the Ansar said to him, "Do you say this while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is among us?" The matter then escalated and was brought to the Prophet (ﷺ), who forbade preferring him over Musa. And he, peace and blessings be upon him, forbade preferring him over Yunus, lest anyone suppose that Yunus, peace be upon him, lacked virtue because of what befell him. Thus his prohibition concerns preferring over a specific person, and his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, in a third hadith: "Do not prefer among the prophets." All of this, together with his saying "I am the master of the descendants of Adam, and I say this without boasting," and the unrestricted attribution of excellence to him without being linked to anyone, is clear and sound. Reflect on this, for it becomes apparent. Indeed, 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to al-Hutay'a: "Praise the one you are praising, and do not prefer some people over others."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The expression "sayyid" (master) and the expression "khayr" (better) are equivalent. This is thus another principle of reconciling the hadiths which removes the apparent contradiction.

As for His saying, "mughadiban" (in anger): it is said that he became angry with his people when their affair and their obstinacy became prolonged for him, so he departed fleeing by himself. Allah the Exalted had commanded him to remain with them and be patient in calling them, so his sin lay in opposing this command. It is also narrated that he was a young man who could not bear the burdens of prophethood and buckled under them, as a sapling bends under a load. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) was told: ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ [al-Qalam: 48], meaning: be patient and persevere in hardship with your people. Another group said: he was angry with the king who ruled over his people.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is similar to the first in what it attributes to Yunus, peace be upon him. Al-Hasan ibn Abi'l-Hasan and others said: he departed angry with his Lord, and Iblis incited him. They narrated concerning this that when the affair of his people was prolonged for Yunus, peace be upon him, he asked Allah for their punishment. It was said to him: "The punishment will come upon them on such-and-such a day." Yunus, peace be upon him, informed them of this, and they said: "If he departs from us, the punishment will descend; and if he remains among us, we will not care." When the dawn of that day came, Yunus rose and departed, and they became certain of the punishment, so they all went out to the open ground, separated young animals from their mothers, humbled themselves and repented, and Allah removed the punishment from them. Yunus remained in the place to which he had gone out, awaiting news. When he learned that they had not been punished, it grieved him that they regarded him as a liar, and he said: "By Allah, I will never return to them." It is also narrated that it was part of their religion to kill the liar, so he became angry at his Lord and went out on his own way until he entered a ship in the sea.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this account there is weakness that is not hidden, being of a kind that a prophet is not characterized by.

People differed concerning His saying, ﴿fa-zanna an lan naqdira 'alayh﴾ (thinking that We would not decree (any hardship) for him). One group said: Iblis incited him and placed in his thought the possibility that Allah would not have power over him to punish him. 

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a rejected view.

Another group said: the meaning of "zanna an lan naqdira 'alayh" is that He would not constrict his provision on account of his course, from the saying of the Exalted: "Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it" (al-qadr). Another group said: it is from qadar, that is, he thought that He would not decree a punishment upon him. Another group said: the speech is in the form of a question, that is: "Did he think that We would not decree (any hardship) for him?" Mundhir ibn Sa'id reported that some read "afa-zanna" with an alif. Al-Zuhri read "nuqaddira" with a damma on the nun, a fatha on the qaf and a shadda on the dal. Al-Hasan read "fa-zanna an lan yaqdira 'alayh," and also "naqdira." After this statement there is considerable omission, which is elided for its clarification in another verse. The meaning: he entered the sea and so on and so forth, until the fish swallowed him and he was in the darkness of its belly.

People differed concerning the plural "al-zulumat" (the darknesses): what is meant by it? One group said: the darkness of the night, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of the fish. Another group said: the darkness of the sea, the darkness of a fish that swallowed the first fish, and the darkness of the first fish which swallowed Yunus, peace be upon him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is valid to express by "the darknesses" the belly of the first fish alone, as He said: ﴿in the depths of the well﴾ [Yusuf: 15], and all its directions are darkness, so the plural is permissible. It is narrated that Yunus, peace be upon him, prostrated in the belly of the fish when he heard the glorification of the fish at the bottom of the sea, then said in his supplication: "O Allah, I have taken for You a place of prayer in a spot no one has taken before me." And "an" (that) is explanatory, like His saying: "an imshu" (that walk), though this requires consideration. His saying "from the wrongdoers" means: in what he opposed, by abandoning persistence with his people and patience with them. This is the best of the interpretations, and others have been mentioned earlier. So Allah answered him and brought him out onto dry land, and the description of this will come in its place. "Al-ghamm" (the distress) is what he suffered when the fish swallowed him.

The majority of reciters read "nunji" with two nuns, the second being sakin. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read "nujji" with one nun, damma, and a shadda on the jim, and it is also transmitted from Abu 'Amr. A group read "nunajji" with two nuns, the first damma, the second fatha, and the jim shadda. As for the first and third readings, both are clear: the first's verb is transitive by the hamza, and the other by doubling. As for the middle reading, which has one nun with damma, a shadda on the jim, and a sakin ya', Abu 'Ali said: it has no basis, and it is merely a mistake of the hearer. This is because 'Asim recited "nunji" and the second nun cannot be pronounced clearly, since it is concealed before these letters, meaning the jim and what runs in its course; so the concealment resembles assimilation. It is impossible that the original was "nunji," and then the meeting of the two nuns led to assimilating one into the jim, since the meeting of two identical letters only calls for that when their vowels are the same. It is also impossible that the original was "nunajji" with the ya' sukun and the passive verb's object being the infinitive, as if he said: "the deliverance was delivered to the believers," since this occurs only in poetic necessity and is not in the Book of Allah the Exalted. The evidence for it is the line of the poet:

"Even if Qufayra had given birth to a whelp of a dog, the dogs would have been reviled on account of that whelp."

Also, the passive verb, when in the past tense, does not have its final letter sukun.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The mushafs contain one nun, written thus because the second nun is concealed.

All of this, together with his saying "I am the master of the descendants of Adam, and I say this without boasting," and the unrestricted attribution of excellence to him without being linked to anyone, is clear and sound. Reflect on this, for it becomes apparent. Indeed, 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to al-Hutay'a: "Praise the one you are praising, and do not prefer some people over others."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The expression "sayyid" (master) and the expression "khayr" (better) are equivalent. This is thus another principle of reconciling the hadiths which removes the apparent contradiction.

As for His saying, "mughadiban" (in anger): it is said that he became angry with his people when their affair and their obstinacy became prolonged for him, so he departed fleeing by himself. Allah the Exalted had commanded him to remain with them and be patient in calling them, so his sin lay in opposing this command. It is also narrated that he was a young man who could not bear the burdens of prophethood and buckled under them, as a sapling bends under a load. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) was told: ﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾ [al-Qalam: 48], meaning: be patient and persevere in hardship with your people. Another group said: he was angry with the king who ruled over his people.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is similar to the first in what it attributes to Yunus, peace be upon him. Al-Hasan ibn Abi'l-Hasan and others said: he departed angry with his Lord, and Iblis incited him. They narrated concerning this that when the affair of his people was prolonged for Yunus, peace be upon him, he asked Allah for their punishment. It was said to him: "The punishment will come upon them on such-and-such a day." Yunus, peace be upon him, informed them of this, and they said: "If he departs from us, the punishment will descend; and if he remains among us, we will not care." When the dawn of that day came, Yunus rose and departed, and they became certain of the punishment, so they all went out to the open ground, separated young animals from their mothers, humbled themselves and repented, and Allah removed the punishment from them. Yunus remained in the place to which he had gone out, awaiting news. When he learned that they had not been punished, it grieved him that they regarded him as a liar, and he said: "By Allah, I will never return to them." It is also narrated that it was part of their religion to kill the liar, so he became angry at his Lord and went out on his own way until he entered a ship in the sea.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this account there is weakness that is not hidden, being of a kind that a prophet is not characterized by.

People differed concerning His saying, ﴿fa-zanna an lan naqdira 'alayh﴾ (thinking that We would not decree (any hardship) for him). One group said: Iblis incited him and placed in his thought the possibility that Allah would not have power over him to punish him. 

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a rejected view.

Another group said: the meaning of "zanna an lan naqdira 'alayh" is that He would not constrict his provision on account of his course, from the saying of the Exalted: "Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it" (al-qadr). Another group said: it is from qadar, that is, he thought that He would not decree a punishment upon him. Another group said: the speech is in the form of a question, that is: "Did he think that We would not decree (any hardship) for him?" Mundhir ibn Sa'id reported that some read "afa-zanna" with an alif. Al-Zuhri read "nuqaddira" with a damma on the nun, a fatha on the qaf and a shadda on the dal. Al-Hasan read "fa-zanna an lan yaqdira 'alayh," and also "naqdira." After this statement there is considerable omission, which is elided for its clarification in another verse. The meaning: he entered the sea and so on and so forth, until the fish swallowed him and he was in the darkness of its belly.

People differed concerning the plural "al-zulumat" (the darknesses): what is meant by it? One group said: the darkness of the night, the darkness of the sea, and the darkness of the fish. Another group said: the darkness of the sea, the darkness of a fish that swallowed the first fish, and the darkness of the first fish which swallowed Yunus, peace be upon him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is valid to express by "the darknesses" the belly of the first fish alone, as He said: ﴿in the depths of the well﴾ [Yusuf: 15], and all its directions are darkness, so the plural is permissible. It is narrated that Yunus, peace be upon him, prostrated in the belly of the fish when he heard the glorification of the fish at the bottom of the sea, then said in his supplication: "O Allah, I have taken for You a place of prayer in a spot no one has taken before me." And "an" (that) is explanatory, like His saying: "an imshu" (that walk), though this requires consideration. His saying "from the wrongdoers" means: in what he opposed, by abandoning persistence with his people and patience with them. This is the best of the interpretations, and others have been mentioned earlier. So Allah answered him and brought him out onto dry land, and the description of this will come in its place. "Al-ghamm" (the distress) is what he suffered when the fish swallowed him.

The majority of reciters read "nunji" with two nuns, the second being sakin. 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read "nujji" with one nun, damma, and a shadda on the jim, and it is also transmitted from Abu 'Amr. A group read "nunajji" with two nuns, the first damma, the second fatha, and the jim shadda. As for the first and third readings, both are clear: the first's verb is transitive by the hamza, and the other by doubling. As for the middle reading, which has one nun with damma, a shadda on the jim, and a sakin ya', Abu 'Ali said: it has no basis, and it is merely a mistake of the hearer. This is because 'Asim recited "nunji" and the second nun cannot be pronounced clearly, since it is concealed before these letters, meaning the jim and what runs in its course; so the concealment resembles assimilation. It is impossible that the original was "nunji," and then the meeting of the two nuns led to assimilating one into the jim, since the meeting of two identical letters only calls for that when their vowels are the same. It is also impossible that the original was "nunajji" with the ya' sukun and the passive verb's object being the infinitive, as if he said: "the deliverance was delivered to the believers," since this occurs only in poetic necessity and is not in the Book of Allah the Exalted. The evidence for it is the line of the poet:

"Even if Qufayra had given birth to a whelp of a dog, the dogs would have been reviled on account of that whelp."

Also, the passive verb, when in the past tense, does not have its final letter sukun.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The mushafs contain one nun, written thus because the second nun is concealed.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 89–90:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And Zakariyya, when he called out to his Lord: "My Lord, do not leave me alone (without an heir), and You are the best of inheritors."﴾ ﴿So We responded to him, and We gave him Yahya, and We made his wife fit for him. Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds, and they would call upon Us in hope and in fear, and they were humbly submissive to Us.﴾

The matter of Zakariyya (peace be upon him) has preceded in Surat Maryam, and (so has) the rectifying of the wife. It has been said: by making her able to conceive while she was barren, so she menstruated and conceived; and this is what resembles the verse. It has also been said: by removing a foulness that was in her tongue.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is weak, and the general wording encompasses every aspect of rectification.

One group read: "wa-yad'unana" (وَيَدْعُونَنا), another group read: "wa-yad'unâ" (وَيَدْعُونا), and another group read: "raghaban" (رَغَبًا) with a fatha on the ra' and the ghayn, and "wa-rahaban" (وَرَهَبًا) likewise. Another group read both with a damma on the ra' and a sukun on the ghayn and the ha', and another group read with a fatha on the ra' and a sukun on the ghayn and the ha'. The meaning is that they call upon Him at the time of their worship while in a state of desire and hope, and of awe and fear, all at once; because desire and awe are mutually connected. Some people said: "raghab" is to raise the palms of the hands toward the sky, and "rahab" is to raise their backs.

The judge Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The summary of this is that the habit of every human supplicant is to use his hands. So "raghab," insofar as it is seeking, is appropriate with it: one opens the inner part of the palm toward the one from whom one seeks, since it is the place of giving and by it one takes possession. And "rahab," insofar as it is the repelling of harm, is appropriate with it: casting that aside, and indicating its going away and its avoidance by shaking out the two hands or the like.

And "khushu'" (الخُشُوعُ): humble submission of the body that is built upon humble submission of the heart.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And she who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our spirit, and We made her and her son a sign for the worlds.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.﴾ ﴿But they divided their affair among themselves into sects; each of them will be returned to Us.﴾ ﴿So whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer, his striving will not be denied, and indeed We are recording it for him.﴾ ﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they should not return.﴾

The meaning: Mention her who guarded her chastity (*aḥṣanat farjahā*), namely Maryam daughter of 'Imran, mother of 'Isa, peace be upon them both. The *farj* (the private part), according to the majority of scholars, and this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, is the well-known body part, and her guarding it is praise. A group said: the *farj* here is the opening of her garment from which the angel breathed. This is weak. As for the breathing of the child into her, many scholars said: He only breathed into the collar of her shirt (*jayb dir'ihā*). The "spirit" (*al-rūḥ*) is attributed to Him by the attribution of ownership to the owner. "Her son" is 'Isa son of Maryam, peace be upon him. The Exalted intended that He made the whole story of 'Isa and the story of Maryam, peace be upon them both, from its beginning to its end, a sign for whoever takes heed of it. "For the worlds" means: for those who lived at that time and those after them.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours﴾ may be a disconnected (*munqaṭi'*) speech, addressed to the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ). Then He informed about the people that they divided into sects, then He promised and threatened. It may also be connected (*muttaṣil*), meaning: We made Maryam and her son a sign for the worlds by sending to them a religion (*milla*) and a book, and it was said to them: ﴿Indeed, this community of yours﴾, that is, he called all of them to belief in Allah, blessed and exalted, and to worshipping Him. Then the Exalted informed that after that they differed and divided their affair into sects. Then He distinguished between the good-doer and the wrongdoer. He mentioned the good-doer with promise, meaning: whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer, he will be rewarded for his striving. He mentioned the wrongdoer with threat in His saying: ﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed﴾, the verse. So consider the threat in it under every opinion, as a reminder, for it is clear. *Al-kufrān* is a verbal noun like *al-kufr* (ingratitude/denial), and from it is the saying of the poet:

"I saw people whose cheeks do not sleep,
and my cheek, and there is no *kufrān* of Allah sleeping."

The reciters differed regarding His saying, the Exalted: *wa-ḥarām*. 'Ikrima and others read *wa-ḥaramun* with a fatha on the *ḥā'* and a kasra on the *rā'*. The majority of the Seven read *wa-ḥarāmun*. Ḥamza, al-Kisa'i, and Ḥafs from 'Asim read *wa-ḥirmun* with a kasra on the *ḥā'* and a sukun on the *rā'*. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read (according to one report from him) *wa-ḥarmun* with a fatha on the *ḥā'* and a sukun on the *rā'*. A group read *wa-ḥarrama* with a fatha on the *ḥā'* and the *rā'* and a shadda on the *rā'*. A group read *wa-ḥurrima* with a damma on the *ḥā'*, a kasra on the *rā'*, and a shadda. Qatada and Maṭar al-Warraq read *wa-ḥaruma* with a fatha on the *ḥā'* and a damma on the *rā'*. The most widespread of these readings are the reading of the one who reads *wa-ḥirmun* and the reading of the one who reads *wa-ḥarāmun*, and both are verbal nouns, like *al-ḥill* and *al-ḥalāl* (lawful).

As for the meaning of the verse: a group said: *ḥarām* and *ḥirm* mean: a firm and decisive judgment upon a town which We destroyed, that they will not return to the world to repent and be given the chance to make amends. Rather, they are heading to punishment. Some of this group said: "destruction" (*al-ihlāk*) is by the sealing of hearts and the like, and "return" (*al-rujū'*) is return to repentance and belief. Another group said: the meaning is: *wa-ḥarām*, that is, prohibited (*mumtani'*), and *ḥirm* likewise, upon a town which We destroyed that they should not return. They said: there is no addition (*ziyāda*) in the speech. They differed regarding "destruction" and "return" according to the two opinions mentioned. Abu 'Ali said: It is possible that *ḥarām* is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), with their return as the predicate (*khabar*), and *lā* is superfluous. It is also possible that *ḥarām* is in the nominative as the predicate of a subject, as if he said: the cancellation (*iqāla*) and repentance are forbidden. Then the meaning would be "that they do not return," so *lā* keeps its original function, as if he said: this is impossible for them because of such-and-such. So the prohibition in the verse is a general one; it is not like the prohibition of the Law, which, if the one forbidden wishes, he may commit.

A meaning is apparent in the verse, within which there is a clear threat. That is, He mentioned the one who does righteous deeds while being a believer, then returned to mentioning the disbelievers who, because of their disbelief and belief, hold that they will not be gathered to a Lord and will not return to a Resurrection. They therefore assume that no punishment will reach them. So the verse came refuting the assumption of these people, meaning: it is impossible for the destroyed disbelievers that they should not be returned; rather, they are returning to the punishment of Allah and His painful torment. So *lā* keeps its original function, and *ḥarām* keeps its original meaning, and likewise *ḥirm*. So reflect on it.
