Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 96–97:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Until, when Gog and Magog are let loose, and they come swarming from every hillock.﴾ ﴿And the true promise draws near, and behold, the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare fixedly: "Woe to us! We were heedless of this. Nay, we were wrongdoers."﴾

"Until" (ḥattā) in this verse may be connected to His words "and they will be cut off" (wa-taqaṭṭaʿū). It may also be connected, according to some of the earlier interpretations, to "they will be returned" (yurjaʿūn). It may also be a particle of beginning (ḥarf ibtidāʾ), and this is the most evident, because of "idhā" (when), since it requires an answer, and the answer is what is intended to be mentioned.

Scholars differ here about the answer. One group said the answer is His words "the promise draws near" (iqtaraba al-waʿd), with the wāw being superfluous (zāʾida). Another group, including al-Zajjāj and others, said the answer is in His words, exalted is He, "Woe to us!" (yā waylanā), the meaning being: they said, "Woe to us!", and the wāw is not superfluous. What I say is that the answer is in His words, "then behold, it is staring" (fa-idhā hiya shākhiṣa), and this is the meaning intended to be mentioned, because it is their return, which they used to deny and whose avoidance was forbidden to them.

Al-Jumhūr recited "futiḥat" with a light tā', while Ibn ʿĀmir alone recited "futtiḥat" with a doubled tā'. It is related that Gog and Magog approach the barrier every day and look toward the opening, saying, "Tomorrow it will be opened," without referring the matter to the will of Allah, the Exalted. When tomorrow comes they find the barrier as it was at first, until Allah permits its opening. Then one of them says, "Tomorrow we will open it, if Allah wills," and they find it as they left it, nearly open, and then they open it. ʿĀṣim alone recited "Yaʾjūj wa-Maʾjūj" with a hamza, while al-Jumhūr recited it with facilitation (tasʹhīl). Its explanation was given earlier in Surat al-Kahf, along with much of the condition of Gog and Magog, so we are sufficient here without repeating it.

"Ḥadab" is every raised elevation of the earth, such as a mountain, a hill, a mound, a grave, and the like. One group said that by His words "they" (wa-hum) is meant Gog and Magog, meaning that they will emerge from every high pass and elevation and will cover the earth. This is because of their multitude, to the extent that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah, the Exalted, will say on the Day of Resurrection: 'O Adam, bring forth the portion of the Fire from your offspring.' He will bring out from every thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine." He said: "The people were terrified, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Among you is one man, and from Gog and Magog a thousand men.'" It is also reported that a man among them does not die until he has a thousand children born to him, between men and women. Another group said that by His words "they" is meant the entire world, and that this is only a description of the resurrection from the graves. Ibn Masʿūd recited "min kulli jadath" (from every grave), and this reading supports this interpretation.

"Yanslūn" means: they hasten while descending (yusrigūna fī taṭāmun). From it is the saying of the poet:

Swift as the wolf's gait, when the night grew cold upon him and he slipped away (fa-nasal).

One group read the sīn with a kasra, and another group read it with a ḍamma.

Al-Ṭabarī related on the authority of Abū Saʿīd, who said: "Gog and Magog will come out and will leave no one alive except the people of the fortresses. They will pass by the lake of Tiberias, and its last part will pass by and say: 'There was water here.' Allah will send upon them the nagaf (a worm) until it breaks their necks. The people of the fortresses will say: 'The enemies of Allah have perished.' They will lower a man to look, and he will find them all dead. Then Allah will send down water from the sky, which will cast them into the sea, and He will purify the earth of them." A similar account is in the hadith of Ḥudhayfa, and at its end he said: "And at that time the sun will rise from its west."

It is related that Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, saw children playing and leaping over one another, and said: "This is how the emergence of Gog and Magog will be."

As for His words, "And the true promise draws near," it refers to the Day of Resurrection. It is related in a hadith: "A man will take a colt after Gog and Magog, and he will not reach its benefit until the Hour is established." As for His words "hiya" (it), the view of Sībawayh is that it is a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-qiṣṣa), as if He said: "Then behold, the matter or the event is staring, eyes..." Al-Farrāʾ permitted that it refers to "al-abṣār" (the eyes), which is mentioned by implication of the speech, and what explains it comes afterward, and he cited as evidence:

By her father, my beloved does not say, "Would that Mālik ibn Abī Kaʿb had fled from me!"

Shukhūṣ with the eye means fixing the gaze without blinking, and this befalls one from excessive fear or an illness or the like.

As for His words "Woe to us!", its implied meaning is: "Woe to us! Indeed we were in heedlessness of what we have now found and made clear of the realities." Then they abandoned the first speech and returned to censuring what used to occur to them of deliberately intending disbelief and the purpose of turning away, and so they said: ﴿Nay, we were wrongdoers.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 98–99:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you are to it bound to come.﴾ ﴿Had these been gods, they would not have come to it; and all of them will abide therein.﴾

This is an address to the disbelievers of Makkah, meaning: indeed you and your idols are the fuel (ḥaṣab) of Hell. The "ḥaṣab" (fuel, that with which fire is kindled) is either because it is pelted (tuḥṣabu) with it, i.e., thrown, or it is a term in the language for firewood when it is thrown. As for before it is thrown, it is not called ḥaṣab except by metaphorical extension.

The majority read "ḥaṣabu" with the ṣād vowelled with a fatḥah, while Ibn al-Samayfa' read it with a sukūn. This is by placing the verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of the passive participle (ism al-maf'ūl). ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him), Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, ʿĀ'ishah, and Ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with them all) read "ḥaṭabu Jahannama" with a ṭā'. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) read "ḥaḍabu Jahannami" with a marked ḍād, vowelled with a fatḥah, while many others read it with a sukūn. The "khaḍab" also means what is thrown into the fire so that it is kindled by it, and the "miḥḍab" is the stick with which the fire is stirred, or the iron rod and the like. From this is the saying of al-A'shā:

"So do not be, in our war, one who stirs the fire, lest you make your people into scattered tribes."

His saying, the Exalted: "what you worship" intends the idols, and their being burned with fire is by way of rebuke to their worshippers. Since "mā" may in some contexts be used for those who have intellect, ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zibaʿrā objected to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ regarding this verse, saying: Indeed ʿĪsā, ʿUzayr and the like have been worshipped besides Allah, so it follows that they would be fuel for Hell. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already preceded from Us﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 101], and so on. Then He affirmed the matter by pointing to the idols which he had seen in His saying "what you worship", and said: ﴿Had these been gods, they would not have come to it﴾. He expressed the idols with "these" (hā'ulā') from the standpoint that they, in their view, are in the condition of those who have intellect. And "al-wurūd" in this verse is the wurūd of entering.

As for before it is thrown, it is not called ḥaṣab except by metaphorical extension.

The majority read "ḥaṣabu" with the ṣād vowelled with a fatḥah, while Ibn al-Samayfa' read it with a sukūn. This is by placing the verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of the passive participle (ism al-maf'ūl). ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him), Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, ʿĀ'ishah, and Ibn al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with them all) read "ḥaṭabu Jahannama" with a ṭā'. Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) read "ḥaḍabu Jahannami" with a marked ḍād, vowelled with a fatḥah, while many others read it with a sukūn. The "khaḍab" also means what is thrown into the fire so that it is kindled by it, and the "miḥḍab" is the stick with which the fire is stirred, or the iron rod and the like. From this is the saying of al-A'shā:

"So do not be, in our war, one who stirs the fire, lest you make your people into scattered tribes."

His saying, the Exalted: "what you worship" intends the idols, and their being burned with fire is by way of rebuke to their worshippers. Since "mā" may in some contexts be used for those who have intellect, ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zibaʿrā objected to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ regarding this verse, saying: Indeed ʿĪsā, ʿUzayr and the like have been worshipped besides Allah, so it follows that they would be fuel for Hell. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already preceded from Us﴾ [al-Anbiyā’: 101], and so on. Then He affirmed the matter by pointing to the idols which he had seen in His saying "what you worship", and said: ﴿Had these been gods, they would not have come to it﴾. He expressed the idols with "these" (hā'ulā') from the standpoint that they, in their view, are in the condition of those who have intellect. And "al-wurūd" in this verse is the wurūd of entering.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 100–103:

The address of His saying, Mighty and Majestic be He:

﴿For them therein is a groaning, and therein they will not hear.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best (al-husna) has preceded from Us—those will be kept far from it.﴾ ﴿They will not hear its faintest sound, and they will abide forever in what their souls desire.﴾ ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them: "This is your day which you were promised."﴾

(p-205) The pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He, "for them" (lahum), refers to those who understand (ya'qilu) from among those who were threatened. And "al-zafir" (groaning) is the sound of one being tormented; it is like the braying of donkeys and the like, except that it comes from the chest. As for His saying, "therein they will not hear," one group said: its meaning is that they will not hear any good or pleasing speech. Another group said: their punishment is that they will be placed in coffins within other coffins, so that there they will hear nothing at all.

When Ibn al-Za'bara objected concerning the matter of 'Isa ibn Maryam and 'Uzayr, the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best has preceded from Us﴾, making clear that these are not included in what is intended, because they did not consent to that and did not call to it. And "al-husna" refers to the word of mercy and the decree of preference. "Al-hasis" is the sound; in general, it is what reaches the senses from the movement of bodies. This is a description of them after their entry into Paradise, because the hadith implies that on the Standing (al-mawqif) Hell will groan a groan such that no prophet or angel remains except that he kneels upon his knees.

"Al-faza' al-akbar" (the greatest terror) is general to every terror that occurs on the Day of Resurrection, so it is as if the Day of Resurrection in its entirety is the greatest terror. And if it is specified with some part of that, it must be intended as the greatest of its horrors. A group said regarding this: it is the slaughtering of Death; another group said: it is the falling of the lid of Hell upon Hell; another group said: it is the command concerning the people of the Fire to the Fire; and another group said: it is the time of the final blast (al-nafkha al-akhira).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This and what preceded it of the times are most fitting to be the time of terror, because it is a time of the hurling of conjectures and the occurrence of events. As for the time of the slaughtering of Death and the falling of the lid of Hell, it is a time when the people of Paradise have already been settled in Paradise; so that is a clear terror that does not afflict anyone of the people of Paradise, let alone the prophets—unless one means: "the thing which, for the people of the Fire, is a greatest terror does not grieve them." But if it is a terror for all, then there is no escape from what we have said, that it is before entry into Paradise.

Some people have gone to the view that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best has preceded from Us﴾ encompasses every believer, and it has been narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "'Uthman is among them."

(p-206) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no doubt that, although it was revealed concerning a specific matter, it encompasses everyone who is granted felicity in the Hereafter.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and the angels will receive them﴾, it means greeting them with peace and giving them good news, i.e., "This is your day, on which you were promised reward and bliss."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 104–105:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿On the day We shall roll up the heaven like the rolling up of the scroll for writings. As We originated the first creation, We shall repeat it; a promise binding upon Us. Indeed, We are ever doing it.﴾ ﴿And We had already written in the Zabur, after the reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants.﴾

A group read "natwī" (نَطْوِي) with the nun of majesty (nūn al-'azama). Another group read "yaṭwī al-samā'" (يَطْوِي السَماءَ) with an open yā', meaning "Allah rolls up". Another group read "tuṭwā" (تُطْوى) with a damma on the tā' and "al-samā'" in the nominative, as a passive form whose agent is not named.

People differed regarding "al-sijjil" (السِجِلِّ). One group said: al-sijjil is an angel who rolls up the pages. Another group said: al-sijjil is a man who used to write for the Prophet (ﷺ). All of this and what resembles it is weak. Another group said: al-sijjil is the sheet on which writing is done, and the meaning of "like the rolling up of the sijjil" is: as the sijjil is rolled up for the sake of the writing that is in it. Here the verbal noun (maṣdar) is in construct with the object. It may also be that the verbal noun is in construct with the subject, meaning: as the sijjil rolls up the writing that is in it. It is as if he said: on the day We roll up [the heaven] in the manner in which the sijjil is rolled up for the writing; so there is a figurative usage (tajawwuz) in the comparison.

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan read "al-sijli" (السِجْلِ) with a shadda on the sīn, sukūn on the jīm and lightening of the lām. Abu al-Samāl opened the sīn and read it "al-sajla" (السَجْلَ). Abu Zur'a ibn 'Amr ibn Jarīr read "al-sujul" (السُجُلُ) with a damma on the sīn, shadda on it, and damma on the jīm. The majority read "lil-kitāb" (لِلْكِتابِ), while Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī and Ḥafṣ from 'Āṣim read "lil-kutub" (لِلْكُتُبِ).

His exalted saying: ﴿As We originated the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾ may carry two meanings. The first is that it is a report about the resurrection: as We invented the first creation without a model, so We shall bring them into being again at another time, and We shall raise them from the graves. The second is that it is a report that every person will be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection in the form in which he came out into the world. This interpretation is supported by the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked and uncircumcised, as We originated the first creation, We shall repeat it." (p-207) The kāf in His saying "kamā bada'nā" is connected to His saying "nu'īduh". His saying: ﴿Indeed, We are ever doing it﴾ is an emphasis of the matter, meaning that the matter in which this is is binding.

A group said: "al-Zabūr" is a term that encompasses all the revealed books, because it is derived from "zabartu al-kitāb", meaning "I wrote the book." Another group said: "al-dhikr" refers to the Preserved Tablet, and some of them said: the dhikr that is in the heaven. Another group said: al-Zabūr is the Zabur of Dawud, peace be upon him, and al-dhikr refers to the Torah. Another group said: al-Zabūr is what came after the Torah of the books, and al-dhikr is the Torah. Ḥamza alone read "al-Zubūr" (الزَبُورَ) with a damma on the zāy.

A group said: "al-arḍ" (the earth) refers to the earth of this world, meaning every part of the earth that the believers attain. Another group said it refers to the earth of Paradise, citing His blessed and exalted saying: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and has caused us to inherit the earth, to settle in Paradise wherever we will."﴾ [al-Zumar: 74]. Another group said that this verse was revealed only to inform about what He had done with the Children of Israel; that is: know that We were faithful to them in what We had promised them, and likewise We shall fulfil for you what We have promised you of victory.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 106–109:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, in this is a message for a people who worship.﴾ ﴿And We have not sent you, [O Muhammad], except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾ ﴿Say, "It has only been revealed to me that your God is but one God, so will you submit?"﴾ ﴿And if they turn away, then say, "I have announced to you equally, and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far."﴾

A group said: The reference in His saying, Exalted is He, "in this" (fi hadha), is to these preceding verses. Another group said: The reference is to the Qur'an in its entirety, and worship (ʿibadah) includes faith in God, Exalted is He. As for His saying, ﴿except as a mercy to the worlds﴾, one group said: "the worlds" is general, but He means only those who believed, because the Prophet (ﷺ) is not a mercy to those who disbelieved in him and died in their disbelief. Another group said: "the worlds" is general and his mercy to the believers is evident, while for the disbelievers it is that God, Exalted is He, lifted from the nations that there should befall them what used to befall the generations before them of types of punishment that uproot, such as the Flood and other than it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The statement may mean: "And We have not sent you to the worlds except as a mercy," that is, he is a mercy in himself and a guidance; whoever takes hold of it takes hold, and whoever turns away from it turns away.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿equally﴾ and "wa in" (and if) means: I have informed you of my warning, and I wanted you to share with me the knowledge of what I have of fear for you from God.

Then He informed them that he does not know the specific time of their punishment, but rather he awaits it, whether near or far, and this is more terrifying and more frightening.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The statement may mean: "And We have not sent you to the worlds except as a mercy," that is, he is a mercy in himself and a guidance; whoever takes hold of it takes hold, and whoever turns away from it turns away.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿equally﴾ and "wa in" (and if) means: I have informed you of my warning, and I wanted you to share with me the knowledge of what I have of fear for you from God.

Then He informed them that he does not know the specific time of their punishment, but rather he awaits it, whether near or far, and this is more terrifying and more frightening.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 21, verses 110–112:

God, the Exalted and Majestic, said:

﴿He surely knows what is spoken aloud and He knows what you conceal.﴾ ﴿And I do not know, perhaps it is a trial for you and a provision for a time.﴾ ﴿He said, "My Lord, judge with truth. Our Lord is the Most Merciful, the One whose help is sought against what you describe."﴾

The pronoun in His words "innahu" ("surely He") refers to God, Exalted is He. In this verse there is a threat, meaning: He knows all the things you do, and He is watching to requite you for them.

Yahya ibn 'Amir read "wa-in adri la'allahu" and "wa-in adri aqarib" with a fatha on the ya' in both. Ibn Mujahid denied the fatha on this ya', and Abu al-Fath gave it a justification.

(p. 209) His words, "la'allahu" (perhaps it): the pronoun in it refers to the respite granted to them, to God's pardoning them from His punishment, and to the continuation of blessings upon them. "Fitnah" (trial) means testing and affliction, and "al-mata'" (provision) means that which is enjoyed during the duration of the life of this world.

Then God commanded him to say, by way of supplication: ﴿My Lord, judge with truth.﴾ Supplicating with this here contains a threat, meaning: the truth is only my victory over you. God's command to make this supplication is a sign of the answering of it and a promise of it.

A group read "Rabbi uhkum" (with the verb in the imperative, without the "qul"). Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "Rabbu" with a ḍammah as a vocative of a singular noun (al-munada al-mufrad, the addressed singular noun). A group read "Rabbiya ahkamu" in the pattern af'alu, following the structure of al-ibtida' wa-l-khabar (the nominal sentence of subject and predicate). A group read "Rabbi ahkama" as a past-tense verb. The meanings of these readings are clear.

Then, at the end of the verse, he placed his trust and sought help from God, the Exalted. The majority of reciters read "qul rabbi uhkum" (say, "My Lord, judge"). 'Asim, as it is related from him, read "qala rabbi uhkum" (he said, "My Lord, judge"). Ibn 'Amir alone read "'ala ma yasifun" with the ya' (they describe), while the rest of the reciters read "'ala ma tasifun" with the ta' from above, in the second-person address.

The tafsir (exegesis) of Surat al-Anbiya' is complete, and all praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds.
